Mr. Loyden asked the Secretary of State for Energy what steps have been taken to ensure adequate energy supplies in the event of a severe winter.
Mr. Benn: The hazards to fuel and power supplies from cold weather are described below together with the steps taken by Government and industry to anticipate their effects.

In general, the worst hazard affecting the movement of fuel stocks is a combination of heavy snowfall and prolonged severe frost. Heavy snow or severe frost on their own will also affect road and rail movement and the latter can cause problems by freezing up stocks of solid fuel. Inevitably, any sudden onset of severe weather is likely to cause some dislocation of energy supplies before 394 counter measures can have full effect. But with adequate preparedness—by the fuel and transport industries, by local authorities, and on the part of consumers themselves—winter risks can be minimised. They cannot, however, be eliminated and some dislocation is always possible.

The fuel industries, and the transport industries, have contingency plans for reducing the effects of severe cold on the production and distribution of fuel stocks. Responsibility for keeping rail freight moving lies with British Rail. In the event of heavy snowfalls, special trains are available for keeping lines open and heaters have been installed to prevent points from freezing. Local authorities employ resources for keeping roads open under severe winter conditions, and, as with the British Rail, they have over recent years, with guidance from the Department of the Environment, improved their preparations for dealing with these conditions.

Coal. Bad weather is unlikely to interfere with deep-mined production except perhaps in severely affected areas by temporarily reducing the work force available; there has also in the past been the very exceptional case of a pit's winding gear freezing up. At some opencast sites production may be halted temporarily, say by very heavy and continuous rainfall. The main effect of bad weather is on coal movement, 70 per cent. approximately of which is by rail, and the NCB has long experience of the problems which arise. The first aim is to keep all pits and opencast sites working as normally as possible and if movement were restricted, coal would be stocked at or around the pithead or site for accelerated distribution when conditions eased. Generally there is adequate room at pitheads and opencast sites for this purpose.

Each year in October the NCB reviews with British Rail its estimates of winter production and the railway resources available to move it. Contingency plans to transfer movement temporarily to road are then brought up to date and detailed consultations take place at regional and
395 area level with railway officers and main consumers. Following this the Joint NCB/BR Policy Committee meets to consider and approve the overall contingency plans.

Current stocks of coal at power stations are over 18 million tons—eight weeks' at normal winter rates of consumption. The British Steel Corporation and industry generally have about seven to eight weeks' supply, and coal merchants about four weeks', apart from certain grades, e. g. anthracite. All this represents normal or above average stocks. In the event of serious interruption of deliveries from the pits the NCB would take steps to direct supplies to priority customers such as hospitals, schools and other essential services.

Gas. The British Gas Corporation expects to be able to cope with severe winter conditions. Ninety-five per cent. of all the gas used in the United Kingdom comes from the North Sea and neither natural gas nor its transmission system is affected by low temperature conditions. Special measures are taken to protect manufactured gas installations against the effects of cold weather. Interruptions in the delivery of naphtha feed-stocks could affect gas manufacture but stocks are adequate and no serious problems are expected, especially as such a low proportion of gas used in this country is manufactured.

Electricity. In the autumn of each year the Electricity Council reviews with the CEGB and the area electricity boards the now well-developed methods for dealing with emergencies in electricity supply to ensure their continued adequacy to deal with the winter ahead. Due to the sharp downturn in the demand for electricity there is at present a considerable amount of spare capacity in the electricity supply system. Unless extremely cold weather arrives unexpectedly the electricity supply system should be able to meet all demands this winter bearing in mind the high stocks of fuel which are available at the power stations. Some consumers, particularly in the remoter 396 regions, may suffer temporary loss of supply if overhead distribution lines are brought down by snow or ice but widespread interruptions of supply are unlikely.

Oil. Much of the oil consumed is transported by pipelines which are not affected by cold. In severe weather the supply of oil by rail to terminals and direct to customers would in general be safeguarded by the measures taken by British Rail, and similarly the measures taken by local authorities to keep roads open should ensure that road tanker deliveries are maintained at a reasonable level. The expectation is, therefore, that even under severe conditions oil should continue to get through in adequate quantities to meet essential needs.

Severe weather will inevitably cause local difficulties and some problems over the supply of particular fuels. If prolonged it could cause inconvenience to any industrial, commercial and domestic consumers who have allowed their stocks of fuel to run down by the time the weather affects distribution. The flexibility of the supply systems used by the energy industries and the special measures employed by British Rail and the local authorities to keep communications open are essential elements in the contingency plans for ensuring that users' essential requirements can continue to be successfully met. All consumers can, however, help to insure against being vulnerable to winter movement difficulties by building up, in advance of the onset of cold weather, the stocks of fuel they hold on their own premises, as is already the practice at power stations and steelworks.

Mr. Dudley Smith asked the Secretary of State for Energy to what extent in his campaign to save energy he is making use of the Building Research Station, Fire Research Station and Princes Risborough Laboratory to test and provide impartial assessments of the various materials and
397 techniques which can be used for the better insulation of buildings.
Mr. Freeson: I have been asked to reply.
Such assessments are made by the Agreement Board, to which the three research establishments in question all give technical support.

32. Sir D. Renton asked the Secretary of State for Industry if he will give a general direction to the Post Office to introduce a uniform rate for daytime telephone calls, in view of the congestion caused in the afternoon by the present arrangements for cheaper calls at that time.

Mr. Gregor Mackenzie: No. The management of the tariff structure to even out demand is a matter for the day-to-day management of the Post Office. In any event, I am advised that over the country as a whole traffic in the morning is still slightly higher than in the afternoon.

Mr. Tom King asked the Secretary of State for Industry what figures are available on postal traffic volumes following the latest price increase; and how these compare with the traffic levels for the comparable period last year.

Mr. Gregor Mackenzie: The Post Office tells me that, based on its normal statistical sampling methods—which exclude metered mail—it estimates that total volume of traffic during the period 28th September to 25th October 1975 has declined by 13·0 per cent. compared with the same period in 1974.

Mr. Tom King asked the Secretary of State for Industry what are the proportions of first- and second-class mail after the latest price increase, before the latest price increase and for the comparable period last year.

Mr. Gregor Mackenzie: The Post Office tells me that over the period from 28th September to 25th October 1975, 38·7 per cent. of letter traffic was sent first class and 61·3 per cent. second class. I am also informed that over the same period in 1974, 48·1 per cent. was sent first class and 519 per cent. second class.

Figures for the period immediately preceding the tariff increases are not available; the nearest period for which figures are available is the month of August 1975 when 40·9 per cent. of letter mail was sent first class and 59·1 per cent. second class. Over the same period in 1974, 48·8 per cent. of letter mail was sent first class and 51·2 per cent. second class.
These figures exclude throughout mail franked by users' own postage meter machines.

Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of State for Industry if he will detail in percentage terms the total of price rises in every one of the nationalised industries with which his Department was concerned during the past 12 months.

Mr. Kaufman: There was an average 20 per cent. rise in the prices of the British Steel Corporation's Treaty of Paris products on 2nd January 1975. BSC made price increases and also introduced price rebates on selected products in June 1975, and made further price increases on selected products of between 5 per cent. and 8·5 per cent. on 26th October 1985. Full details are given in the Corporation's price lists.
Following is the information for the Post Office—all increases are weighted averages:
Telecommunications (28th April–1st May 1975) +35 per cent.
Telecommunications (1st October 1975) +33 per cent.
Posts (17th March 1975) +47 per cent.
Posts (29th September 1975) +22·5 per cent.

Mr. Tom King asked the Secretary of State for Industry if he will publish in
399 the Official Report figures illustrating his conclusion that the substance of the problem of Post Office deficits was caused by uneconomic tariffs in the years 1971 to 1974.
Mr. Gregor Mackenzie: Post Office tariff applications between 1971 and 1974 were tailored to meet the requirements of successive stages of price restraint.

The following statements indicate for the two main businesses. Telecommunications and Posts, the extent to which the yield from price increases in the years 1971–72 to 1974–75 fell short of the amount estimated to be required, when the price proposals were formulated, simply to break even.
The amount of this shortfall reflects the operation successively of the CBI restraint

policy, of the Price Codes as interpreted by the Price Commission and of Government policy as to Post Office prices, together with the delays inherent in the consultative/approval processes. The Post Office sought throughout to introduce the maximum price increases permissible within the limits operating at the time.

The statements also show that the actual deficits have generally exceeded the amount of the shortfall as described above. This is mainly because inflation proved greater than could be allowed for in the price increases.
All the figures quoted are for the inland services only, since the prices for international services have not been limited by the price codes.

Mr. Gorst asked the Secretary of State for Industry when he expects to announce the terms and membership of the inquiry into the Post Office; and on what dates the inquiry will be started and completed.
Mr. Gregor Mackenzie: My right hon. Friend hopes to make an announcement shortly and I must ask the hon. Member to await that announcement.

Mr. Tom King asked the Secretary of State for Industry whether he is yet able to announce the outcome of his discussions on the problem of the Post Office Pension Fund deficit; and what guidance he has given to the Post Office on the treatment of this deficit in their forward financial planning.

Mr. Gregor Mackenzie: As the hon. Member will be aware, the decision taken in respect of 1975–76 has been announced. Discussions have been held with the Post Office and the unions affected on what should be done in respect of future years and a decision will be announced as soon as possible. The Post Office's financial planning necessarily includes alternative provision for a wide range of contingencies.

Mr. Tom King asked the Secretary of State for Industry how many public relations officers were employed by his Department in March 1974; how many are employed now; whether he expects to recruit any more during the rest of 1975 and 1976; and what are the salaries of those he has recruited and expects to recruit.

Mr. Kaufman: The number of information officers in the Department on 31st March 1974 was 53. The number currently in post is unchanged, and there has been no decision either to increase or decrease the number employed. At all relevant times some common services have been provided for the Departments of Trade and Prices and Consumer Protection.
Mr. Corrie asked the Secretary of State for Industry what is the maximum allocation allowable to the United Kingdom from the EEC Regional Development Fund.
Mr. Gregor Mackenzie: About £150 million for 1975–77.
Mr. Corrie asked the Secretary of State for Industry how many firms have applied for assistance from the Regional Development Fund; and what is the total amount involved.
Mr. Gregor Mackenzie: Applications are submitted by Governments. We have put in applications totalling rather more than our 1975 quota.

Mr. Cant asked the Secretary of State for Industry whether, in view of the fact that the £26·7 million injected into Alfred Herbert has been used up in the purchase of ordinary shares and the repayment of debts and borrowings, he will now publish an estimate of any further amount that will be required to complete rationalisation and reorganisation, and provide finance for new investment.

Mr. Gregor Mackenzie: The financial assistance to be provided to Alfred Herbert, by subscription for £26,179,765 share capital, awaits approval by the ordinary shareholders of the proposed scheme of arrangement, sanction of the scheme by the court and the enactment of the Industry Bill. I expect that the £25 million included within this sum as new long-term finance will enable the company to embark on the necessary rationalisation, reorganisation and new investment. The need for any further finance will thereafter be a matter for consideration by the company in consultation with the National Enterprise Board.

Mr. Grist asked the Secretary of State for Industry if he will list for each of the last three years the number of civil servants in his Department who have been prematurely retired on grounds of (i) inefficiency, (ii) limited efficiency, (iii) redundancy and (iv) discipline, showing executive and administrative grades separately.

Mr. Kaufman: Since this Department was formed on 5th March 1974, only one officer in the Administration Group—Executive Officers and above—has been retired prematurely on any of the grounds indicated—in 1975 on disciplinary grounds.

Mr. Cordle asked the Secretary of State for Industry what assistance his Department has given to the textile industry since January 1975; what further assistance is planned for the next 12 months: and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Kaufman: I refer the hon. Member to the statement made by my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for Industry on 23rd July [Official Report, 23rd July 1975; Vol. 896, c. 558–71.]. I also refer the hon. Member to the reply given to my hon. Friend the Member for Sowerby (Mr. Madden) [Official Report, 24th October 1975, Vol. 898, c. 296–7.]

In amplification of the reply given to my hon. Friend, I give below the figures showing identifiable financial assistance to the textile industry since 1st January 1975.
a. Payments under Section 7 of the Industry Act 1972 (£000s) 1st January 1975 to date £1,095.
b. Regional Development Grants (£000s). Figures are not available from 1st January 1975. Payments from 1st April–30th September 1975 were £4,300.
c. Payments under the Wool Textile Scheme, Section 8 of the Industry Act 1972 (£000s). 1st January to date, £3,700.

Since January 1975 restraint agreements on trade in yarns, textiles and made-ups have been concluded under the GATT Multi-Fibre Arrangement with India, Pakistan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Macao and Malaysia. Restraints have been imposed on Taiwan and South Korea. During the next 12 months negotiations for restraint agreements will be held with Brazil, Colombia, Mexico, Yugoslavia and other Eastern Area countries.
The full range of the Department's facilities will continue to be made available to the textile industry during the next 12 months.
Mr. Wells asked the Secretary of State for Industry what representations he has had from management or unions of the Maidstone plant of Chrysler (UK) Ltd., as opposed to the company as a whole.
Mr. Kaufman: None.

Mr. Tomlinson asked the Secretary of State for Industry whether he will now publish the Appendices to the Report entitled "Strategy Alternatives for the British Motor Cycle Industry" which was published as House of Commons Paper 532.

Mr. Kaufman: Because of their undoubted value and interest I have decided to publish these appendices, subject to the exclusion of confidential material, as a part to this report (532/1). Copies are being placed today in the Libraries and in the Vote Office and Printed Paper Office.
Mr. Golding asked the Secretary of State for Industry whether he intends to relax any of the constraints placed on the activities of Cable and Wireless Limited in the United Kingdom.

Mr. Varley: Yes. I have agreed to relax the restrictions placed by the previous Government on Cable and Wireless's freedom to provide telecommunications private systems and allied services in the United Kingdom, subject to consultation with the Government on significant developments. I believe that the company has a great deal to offer and that it is important that it should be free to compete with the private sector on an equal footing.

Mr. Richard Wainwright asked the Secretary of State for Industry how many accidents involving fatalities occurred on British Railways during the last 12 months; how many people lost their lives; and what percentage of the total number of passengers carried this figure represents.
Dr. Gilbert: I have been asked to reply.
Two train accidents, in which five passengers lost their lives. This represents less than a millionth of 1 per cent. of passenger journeys.
33. Mr. Thorne asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he is satisfied with the present methods of disposing of nuclear waste; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Denis Howell: Yes. Extensive monitoring confirms that discharges to the environment are being kept to a safe level.

Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what are the total funds that have been set aside by British Rail for capital investment during the current year; and how much has been allocated for station modernisation and electrification.

Dr. Gilbert: Investment in the railway and ancillary activities of the Railways Board should be about £237 million at mid-1975 prices—including £9·5 million on station modernisation and £9·4 million on eletrification.
Mr. D. E. Thomas asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what is his estimate of the number of persons who have become eligible for rate rebates as a result of increased savings disregard.
Mr. Oakes: It is not envisaged that the increase in the amount of uninvested savings which is disregarded will have any appreciable effect on the number of persons who are eligible for rate rebates.

Mr. Roderick asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what arrangements exist for the allocation or transfer to vehicle owners of vehicle registration numbers and letters of their own choice; what use is made of this facility; and whether he is satisfied with the operation of the arrangements.

Dr. Gilbert: The head of a diplomatic mission may choose for his official car any number which is not in use already—a service which is not much called for and is effectively free. The owners of new busses are given numbers which tally with their bus fleet number. Otherwise, numbers are issued in strict sequence of application for first registration—though numbers which appear likely to give offence or to be highly prized are withheld, and numbers of an appropriate year are found for "vintage" vehicles. For a payment—at present £5·40, including VAT—any vehicle owner may transfer the number of a vehicle in his possession to another which is also in his possession: there are currently some 406 4,500 such "cherished transfers" each month. The arrangements appear to be working reasonably well from a procedural point of view: I am aware that none the less they are the subject of considerable criticism, and I have a review of them in hand at the moment.

Mr. Moate asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will take steps either to end the present temporary speed restrictions or to render them comprehensible to motorists by the erection of appropriate speed limit signs.
Dr. Gilbert: I hope to make a statement very soon.

Mr. Moate asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he can yet make a statement on the effect of imposing additional speed limits on roads in Great Britain for the purposes of energy conservation; what representations he has received about possible confusion caused to motorists; and if it is his intention to continue the present restrictions.
Dr. Gilbert: I hope to make a statement very soon.

Mr. Madden asked the Secretary of State for the Environment whether his order imposing a 50 m.p.h. speed limit on certain roads is intended to inhibit the imposition of lower limits in cases where the relevant authority so desires.
Dr. Gilbert: No; but the replacement of the previous 70 m.p.h. limit by the general 50 m.p.h. limit could have had a bearing on the case for restricting a particular length of road to 40 m.p.h.

Mr. George Rodgers asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he is satisfied that sufficient action is being taken to deal with the silting which is taking place in the Rivers Ribble and Mersey to protect United Kingdom exports which are being hindered by conditions in leaving the ports of Preston and Liverpool.

Dr. Gilbert: Control of siltation in the rivers Ribble and Mersey is a matter for the Port of Preston Authority and the Mersey Docks and Harbour Company respectively. I am informed that they are taking all necessary action.
Mr. Roderick asked the Secretary of State for the Environment how many Government Departments are accommodated in buildings which carry the name "Oldway"; and where they are situated.
Mr Ernest Armstrong: Four Government Departments in eight locations in Wales are accommodated in buildings which carry the name "Oldway".
Details are:
Oldway House, Bargoed Department of Employment (including Employment Services Agency).
Oldway House, Merthyr Tydfil Department of Health and Social Security; Department of the Environment (Driving Test Centre); Her Majesty's Customs and Excise.
Oldway House, Pontypridd Department of Health and Social Security; Department of Employment (including Employment Services Agency).
Oldway House, Perth Department of Health and Social Security.
Oldway Centre, Swansea Department of the Environment (Driver and Vehicle Licensing Centre).
Oldway House, Swansea Department of Health and Social Security; Her Majesty's Customs and Excise.
Oldway House, Morriston, Swansea Depatment of Health and Social Security.
Oldway House, Treorchy Department of Health and Social Security; Department of Employment (including employment sevices agency); Department of the Environment (Driving Test Centre).

p.quote: In addition Her Majesty's Customs and Excise occupy accommodation at Castle House, Merthyr Tydfil, which is leased from Oldway House development (Pontypridd) Ltd.

body.p: Sir George Young asked the Secretary of State for the Environment whether he will issue regulations requiring motor cyclists' crash helmets to carry reflective and fluorescent material in order to make them more conspicuous.

Dr. Gilbert: Research is in progress into ways of making motor cyclists more conspicuous, including possible modifications to crash helmets. I intend to await the results of this work before considering new regulations.

Mr. Stephen Ross asked the Secretary of State for the Environment whether he is satisfied that the Development Commission is producing sufficient financial assistance to those wishing to establish light industries in rural areas.

Mr. John Silkin: I am satisfied that the Development Commission is making an important contribution to the economic well-being of rural areas. The Government are concerned to see this contribution developed, particularly in order to reduce rural depopulation, and are considering proposals from the Development Commission for the coming years, but current financial stringencies may limit the degree to which this can be done. I would, however, add that part of the £20 million announced by the Chancellor for advance factories for employment creation will be made available to the Development Commission.
Mr. Stephen Ross asked the Secretary of State for the Environment why it is necessary to replace all the trees recently planted in New Palace Yard.

Mr. Armstrong: It was agreed with the Chairman of the Accommodation and Administration Sub-Committee of the Services Committee that the larger trees of the species—Tilia euchlora, which does not exude honey-dew—would be preferable to the common limes already in the Yard. The existing trees will be planted in the Royal Parks.

Mr. Ian Stewart asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will make proposals for dealing with the situation where listed buildings are in a dangerous state and their owners are unable to afford the cost of repairs; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Crosland: It is the responsibility of the appropriate local authority to ensure that action is taken in respect of any building which appears to it to be dangerous. Grants are available to help many owners of listed buildings to meet the cost of repairs, but if the hon. Member has in mind a particular example of difficulty, I will look into it if he writes to me.

Mr. Dudley Smith asked the Secretary of State for the Environment to what extent he is making use of the Building Research Establishment to provide impartial assessments of various building materials and techniques to the building industry at large to assist it in satisfying inquiries related to potential export orders, as well as to assist United Kingdom building.

Mr. Armstrong: Such assessments are the function of the Agreement Board, whose activities have recently been extended to cover traditional materials and techniques, particularly where there is export potential. The Building Research Establishment gives technical support to this board. It also helps the industry through its advisory service, through its substantial contributions to the work of relevant British Standards Institute committees, and by the technical advice it supplies both to this Department, and to the Construction Exports Advisory Board, which is the joint responsibility of the Secretaries of State for the Environment, Trade and Industry.

Mr. Dudley Smith asked the Secretary of State for the Environment whether he is aware that the recent concessions he has made with regard to building byelaws and the filling of cavity walls with insulation will not benefit the 11 million dwellings in the country which do not have cavity walls; and whether he will arrange for additional extensive research and development with regard to the insulation of solid walls by other means.

Mr. Freeson: I attach great importance to the development of a cost-effective method of improving the thermal insulation of existing solid walls. If this could be achieved it would make an important contribution to the more efficient use of energy in buildings. The Building Research Establishment and other organisations are engaged in research on the matter, but so far no economical solution has emerged.

(2) how many applications for bus fare increases were made to the Traffic Commissioners throughout England and Wales during the last 12 months for which figures are available; how many of these applications were altered or amended by the Commissioners; how many applications were rejected; how many applications were approved without alteration; and what average national percentage fare increase the total number of approved applications represented.

Mr. Carmichael: Traffic Commissioners are statutorily independent bodies and this information is not readily available within my Department. I have asked the Commissioners for details and will write to the hon. Member.
Mr. Banks asked the Secretary of State for the Environment on what date he expects to be in a position to make a decision on the proposals for a Pudsey-Dishforth motorway route.

Mr. Carmichael: The results of the public consultation on alternative routes for the proposed new road between Kirkhamgate and Dishforth are at present being analysed. Over 7,500 questionnaires were returned and many other comments received. It is too early yet to say when an announcement about the preferred route can be made.
Mr. Edge asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will introduce legislation to allow local authorities to engage in municipal trading.

Mr. John Silkin: As I told my hon. Friend on 1st August, I sympathise with the general objectives that have prompted his question, and I shall keep in mind the possibility of giving such powers to local authorities when a legislative opportunity offers itself.—[Vol. 896, c. 652.]

Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what is the current period for the removal of an endorsement on a driving licence for: (a) speeding, (b) dangerous driving and (c) driving under the influence of drink and drugs.

Mr. Carmichael: Endorsements for the drinking and driving offences—including driving under the influence of drink or drugs—now remain on licences for eleven years from the date of the order; all others remain for four years. The periods over which earlier convictions count for totting-up purposes—ten years for drinking and driving and three years for other offences—remain unchanged; but the extension of the period of endorsements will ensure that all relevant convictions come to the notice of the courts.

Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what steps have been taken by his Department to ensure that the new time intervals have been brought to the attention of the public pursuant to the Road Traffic Act 1972, Section 101(7), and the Road Traffic Act 1974, Schedule 3, paragraph 10
Mr. Carmichael: The Department issued a Press notice on 10th September 1975, which was reported in most national and many other newspapers.

Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will consider enclosing a leaflet with the issue of new licences to the effect that as from 1st October 1975 endorsements will not be cleared after a three-year interval for speeding and certain other road offences.
Mr. Carmichael: The new periods are referred to in the application form Dl and in the information leaflet D100.
Mr. Frank R. White asked the Secretary of State for the Environment how many Road Fund licences have been issued at the latest convenient date.

Mr. Carmichael: In the twelve months ending 31st August 1975 and in relation to Great Britain, 26·83 million—12·18 million for twelve-month periods and 14·65 million for 4-month periods. The DVLC now holds the records of 4·7 mil- 412 lion vehicles out of an estimated total of 18·1 million.
Mr. Frank R. White asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what is the estimated lost revenue caused by the use of vehicles without a Road Fund licence.
Mr. Carmichael: The best estimate available is some £40 million—though this is based on uncertain evidence.

Mr. Rose asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will list in the Official Report the number of households which have had their water supplies disconnected for the non-payment of bills for each year since 1970.
Mr. Denis Howell: This information is not available.
Mr. Frank R. White asked the Secretary of State for the Environment how many motorists there are in each category of vehicle insurance cover.

Mr. Carmichael: All motor vehicle owners, other than those specified in Section 144 of the Road Traffic Act 1972, are required to have an insurance policy which covers at least their liability for death or bodily injury as specified in Section 145 of the Act. I am informed that, with very few exceptions, all private car policies also include cover against liability for damage to property owned by a third party; and that it is estimated that some 70 per cent. of all policies also include cover against damage to the insured vehicle.
Mr. Frank R. White asked the Secretary of State for the Environment how many driving licences have been issued at the latest convenient date.

Mr. Carmichael: In the twelve months ending 30th September 1975 and in relation to Great Britain, 10,083,791—including 2,845,166 provisional licences valid for one year and 6,356,828 full licences valid for three years: the balance consists of duplicate, exchange and replacement licences. The DVLC now hold the
413 records of 17 million drivers out of an estimated total of 20 million.
Mr. Frank R. White asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what is the estimated lost revenue caused by the use of vehicles without a driver's licence.

Mr. Carmichael: The number oft people driving vehicles without a driving licence is not known. But the fee for a driving licence is designed to cover the cost of producing it—not as a means of producing revenue.

Mr. Fairbairn asked the Secretary of State for the Environment how many times flag poles have been put up in Parliament Square during 1975; how many poles there are; and what was the cost to put each one up and take it down again.

Mr. Armstrong: Poles were put up on three occasions. Sixteen poles were erected for Europe Day and United Nations Day respectively and, exceptionally, 36 poles for the Inter-Parliamentary Union Conference, the cost of which is being reimbursed. The cost varied from £66 to £85 per pole.
Mr. Fairbairn asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what was the cost of each Member's desk supplied to the Norman Shaw North Building.
Mr. Armstrong: The cost of each desk was £178·20.
Mr. Robin F. Cook asked the Secretary of State for the Environment when he hopes to publish the report by Mr. Harold Campbell on housing co-operatives.
Mr. Freeson: By the New Year.

Mr. Ron Lewis asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will undertake to consider the claims of Carlisle in the allocation of the help being made available for the construction industry; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. John Silkin: Yes; if Carlisle has any schemes it would like to be con- 414 sidered, it should get into touch with my Department's regional office.
Mr. Beith asked the Secretary of State for the Environment when he now expects work to start on the Al Felton bypass.
Mr. Carmichael: Subject to the completion of statutory procedures, work is expected to start towards the end of 1976.
Mr. Hatton asked the Secretary of State for the Environment when he expects all the services to be fully restored on the north side of the Corley service area on the M6 motorway.

Mr. Carmichael: I understand that the operating company will fully restore the services on the north-bound side of the Corley service area on the M6 when they consider it safe to do so. I have as yet no information about when this will be since mining operations are still in progress.
Mr. Hatton asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he is satisfied with the standard of lighting at the Corley service area on the M6 motorway.
Mr. Carmichael: Yes.

Mr. Sedgemore asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will publish in the Official Report information on (a) the number of people accepted into temporary accommodation as a consequence of foreclosure by a building society, (b) the number of people in one-parent families included in the above figure and (c) the number of people in the figures above who were in receipt of supplementary benefit at the time of foreclosure; and if he will give this information for each year since 1970.
Mr. Armstrong: I regret this information is not available.

Mr. Sedgemore asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will publish in the Official Report details of (a) the annual number of heads of household in owner occupation who, since the introduction of the option mortgage scheme,
415 have taken advantage of the scheme when entering into a mortgage agreement, (b) the proportion of the total number of heads of household in owner occupation that the above annual figure represents and (c) the annual number of owner occupiers who have transferred from income tax relief to the option scheme after entering into a mortgage agreement.

Mr. Armstrong: About 840,000 option mortgages have been taken out since the scheme began in 1968, but it is not known how many of these were granted to heads of household. Annual details are:
Number of option mortgages Percentages of all mortgages
1968 150,000* —
28,000 7
1969 30,000 5
1970 41,000 7
1971 62,000 9
1972 147,000 21
1973 123,000 21
1974 106,000 21
* Estimated number of mortgagors who switched into the scheme when it was introduced.
No information is available on the annual number of mortgagors who change from a tax relief to an option mortgage, although it is believed to be small.

Sir G. de Freitas asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what were the approximate number of motor car driving licence holders with addresses in the Kettering and Corby districts on 1st January 1975, 1st January 1973, 1st January 1971, and 1st January 1969, respectively.
Mr. Carmichael: I regret that records have not been kept in such a way as to enable the information requested to be supplied.
Mr. Rippon asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what stretching of the time-scale he now envisages for the Kielder water scheme.

Mr. Crosland: The timing of works, and their progress, are matters for the Northumbrian Water Authority. I am informed that the authority has no plans for stretching the time scale for the Kielder water supply scheme, which remains of vital importance to the whole of the region.

Mr. Wells asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what was the expenditure on the Maidstone-Tonbridge A26 trunk road by his Department and by local authorities, respectively, in the financial year 1974–75 and the estimated expenditure in the current year.

Dr. Gilbert: The Maidstone-Tonbridge A26 scheme, which is a principal road scheme, was accepted by the Secretary of State for grant purposes under Section 235(1) of the Highways Act 1959. In 1974–75 the Department paid £7,899 in grant and the local highway authority £2,633.

With the bringing to an end of such specific grants by the Local Government Act 1974 and their replacement from 1st April 1975 by the transport supplementary grant £115,000 was included in
417 respect of this scheme in the total of estimated expenditure accepted by my right hon. Friend for purposes of transport supplementary grant payable to Kent County Council in 1975–76.

Mr. Rippon asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what encouragement is being given to the Housing Corporation to provide student housing accommodation for Newcastle University; what progress is being made; and whether he is supporting similar projects in any other part of the country.

Mr. Crosland: Although the Housing Corporation is aware of plans to convert certain property owned by Newcastle University into accommodation for single young people, including students, no firm proposal has been submitted to it. It would have to consider any such proposal against the claims of other housing schemes put forward by registered housing associations. Similar schemes are being considered in other places where there is a serious shortage of housing for single young people.

Mr. Rippon asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what criteria he has laid down to guide the Housing Corporation in exercising its function under the Housing Act 1974 in order to provide residential accommodation for students; and how much of such accommodation he expects to see provided in the current year.

Mr. Crosland: On 7th May 1975, in answer to a question by the hon. Member for Cambridge (Mr. Lane), the Minister for Housing and Construction made it clear that, although primary responsibility for student accommodation as such rests with the Department of Education and Science, housing association schemes for single young people, including students, will be considered for grant in places where the shortage of student accommodation aggravates the general housing shortage. No estimate is available of the likely provision of such places in the current year—[Vol. 891, c. 448–9.]

Mr. Wells asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will give the total road expenditure in Great Britain by his Department and by local authori- 418 ties, respectively, for the financial year 1974–75.

Dr. Gilbert: Provisional figures for 1974–75 expenditure on new construction, improvement, and maintenance of roads in England show a total of £840 million of which about £440 million was undertaken on behalf of this Department and the remainder by local authorities. My right hon. Friends the Secretaries of State for Scotland and Wales have responsibility for roads expenditure in those countries.

Mr. Wells asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what he estimates to be the total cost to public funds in the current financial year of all public participation exercises and public inquiries related to trunk roads in Great Britain.
Dr Gilbert: I regret that this information is not readily available. I am writing to the hon. Member.

Mr. Wells asked the Secretary of State for the Environment how much land was taken in each of the past 10 years for development in the form of: (a) housing, (b) industry and (c) road development, respectively, in Great Britain.

Mr. John Silkin: This information has not hitherto been collected centrally. Local authorities have however now been asked in DOE Circular 71/74—Welsh Office Circular 114/74—to complete annual statistical returns covering land use changes starting with the year ending 31st March 1976, and these should provide this type of information for the future.

Mr. Frank Allaun asked the Secretary of State for the Environment how many housing action areas and general improvement areas have been established; what are the districts in which they are situated; in how many of these schemes activity has started; how many dwellings are being built or improved in each scheme; and whether any steps are intended to achieve greater results
Mr. Armstrong, pursuant to his reply [Official Report, 20th October 1975; Vol. 898. c. 25–6], gave the following information:

body.p: Mr. Thompson asked the Secretary of State for Scotland how many agricultural workers have been evicted from tied agricultural houses in Scotland in each of the last 10 years and to date in 1975.
Mr. William Ross: Information on evictions from such houses is not available.
Mr. Henderson asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will make a statement on further measures to reform land tenure in Scotland.
Mr. William Ross: I hope to make a statement shortly.
Mr. Donald Stewart asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what was the amount collected in Scotland last year under the teachers' superanuation scheme; and how much was paid out in pensions.
Mr. William Ross: The figures for the financial year 1974–75 are £26,995,079 and £22,593,205, respectively.
Mr. Donald Stewart asked the Secretary of State for Scotland when next he intends to meet representatives of An Comunn Gaidhealach.

Mr. William Ross: My hon. Friend the Under-Secretary of State for Health 454 and Education has written to the Director of An Comuna Gaidhealach, in response to his letter of 7th July, suggesting a meeting with a delegation from An Comunn on a mutually convenient date.

Mr. Michael Latham asked the Secretary of State for Scotland to what legislative or policy factors he attributes the increase in non-industrial staff in his Department from 9,052 on 1st March 1974 to 9,617 on 1st July 1975.

Mr. William Ross: The transfer on 1st July 1975 of staff from the Department of Industry engaged on selective assistance to Scottish industry accounts for more than one-quarter of the increase. A similar proportion of the increase reflects an improvement in recruitment to the Scottish Prison Service and the State Hospital, Carstairs. The remainder is in large measure due to the development of offshore oil and to changes in the administration of superannuation schemes.
Mr. Teddy Taylor asked the Secretary of State for Scotland (1) what plans he has to introduce a new procedure for dealing with complaints against the police; and if he will make a statement;

(2) how many complaints against the police were recorded by Her Majesty's Chief Inspector of Constabulary in 1974; what percentage of these complaints resulted in criminal prosecutions; and what percentage was found to be groundless;
(4) how many letters or representations he has had over the past year about the inadequacy of procedures for dealing with complaints against the police.

Mr. William Ross: Two meetings with representatives of the three police associations and the Convention of Scottish Local Authorities have been held to discuss outline proposals for a new procedure, which will now be put before the Police Advisory Board for Scotland. Until these consultations are complete I cannot usefully make a statement. While the police associations question the need for a change in the present procedure they have made constructive suggestions about the principles which should govern any new scheme to be introduced.

body.p: 35. Mr. Watkinson asked the Secretary of State for Defence, of those who were Absent without leave for more than five years, how many have been discharged without trial and how many have been court-martialled.
Mr. Robert C. Brown: This information is not readily available and could not be provided for any significant period without disproportionate effort.

Mr. Robin F. Cook asked the Secretary of State for Defence if he will list the United Kingdom firms with contracts or pub-contracts on the MRCA airframe, the MRCA aero-engine, and the MRCA avionics, respectively, and the systems or sub-systems for which they are responsible.

Mr. William Rodgers: Subcontract work is spread over a very large number of firms, but the principal airframe, engine and avionic first level subcontractors and the systems or subsystems with which they are associated include the following:

ul.li: BAC Ltd., front, fuselage, rear fuselage, tail.
Ferranti Ltd., inertial navigation system; laser range finder; combined map and radar display.
Decca Navigator Co. Ltd., Doppler navigation radar.
MEASL, main control system; tactical navigation; TV tabulated display; Triplex transducer unit; autopilot and flight director computer; terrain following E-scope display.
Lucas, integrated drive generator; main engine control unit; pitch feel system.
Cossor Electronics Ltd., instrument landing system; IFF transponder.
Smith Industries Ltd., microwave airborne digital; guidance equipment, interface unit; head-up display; horizontal situation indicator.
Ultra Electronics Ltd., communication control system.
S. Davall & Son Ltd., head-up display camera.
Computing Devices Co. Ltd., navigator's weapon aiming mode selector

body.p: Mr. Mather asked the Secretary of State for Defence if he has received representations from the Institute of Professional Civil Servants about the proposed move of staff from the Government offices in Surbiton to Glasgow; and what assurances he has been able to give.

Mr. William Rodgers: I met representatives from several aeronautical quality assurance directorate laboratories, including members of the Institution of Professional Civil Servants from AQD Surbiton, on 7th October 1975 to discuss the proposed dispersal of quality assurance staffs to the Glasgow area. We had a useful exchange of views. I emphasised that no decision had been taken as to which quality assurance staff should be dispersed and I gave an assurance that further discussion would take place with the staff associations and the trades unions concerned; this remains the position.

Mr. Conlan asked the Secretary of State for Defence how many production workers were recruited at the ROF, Birtley, during each of the months January to September 1975; how many were female; how many were young persons; and into which trade classifications the total number fell.

Mr. Robert C. Brown: The numbers of production workers recruited at ROF Birtley between January and September 1975 were:
January 7
February 0
March 3
April 0
May 9
June 41
July 14
August 18
September 53
None of these was female or under 20; the total of 145 was made up of 115 machinists, 15 press operators and 15 foundry workers.

Mr. Hoyle asked the Secretary of State for Defence if he has given any advice to purchasing authorities advising them to purchase textiles which are spun, woven, finished and made up in Great Britain.

Mr. William Rodgers: Instructions have been issued to Ministry of Defence staff concerned with the purchase of textiles or textile products in the United Kingdom to observe the requirements of the statement made by the Secretary of State for Industry on 23rd July 1975.—[Vol. 896, c. 558–60.]

Mr. Townsend asked the Secretary of State for Defence what permanent arrangements are in force in Scotland in case of terrorist attacks on Great Britain's North Sea oil and gas platforms; and to what extent the Royal Marines are participating in such arrangements.

Mr. William Rodgers: The permanent arrangements are those under which the Armed Services provide aid to the civil power as circumstances may require. For Scotland this aid would normally be arranged through the maritime headquarters at Pitreavie and could include Royal Marines.

Mr. Molloy asked the Secretary of State for Defence if he will instigate a full-scale inquiry into allegations of members of Her Majesty's forces being involved in the production of pornographic literature printed overseas; and if he will include in the terms of reference the security aspect.
Mr. Robert C. Brown: Inquiries are in progress following recent Press reports. If any security implications come to light, these will, of course, be investigated.

Mr. McCusker asked the Secretary of State for Defence if he will consider introducing regulations which will mean that an ex-member of the UDR can determine why he has been discharged; and if he will not do so, if he will give his reasons.
Mr. Robert C. Brown: Members of the UDR are informed of the reason for their discharge except where it is against the public interest to do so.

Mr. McCusker asked the Secretary of State for Defence what appeal is available to a member of the UDR against the decision to discharge him if he considers that the decision has been taken as the result of inaccurate intelligence.
Mr. Robert C. Brown: A UDR member who is discharged by his commanding officer may appeal to the Defence Council whatever the reason for discharge.

Mr. McCusker asked the Secretary of State for Defence how many recruits have joined the UDR in County Armagh since 1st January 1975; how many members of the UDR in County Armagh have resigned; and how many have been discharged.

Mr. Robert C. Brown: Records in respect of recruitment to and discharge from part-time service with the Ulster Defence Regiment are not kept on a county by county basis. However, figures are available for 2nd and 11th UDR, the battalions which are based largely, although not exclusively, in County Armagh. These show that 222 members were recruited and 166 discharged during the period 1st January to 31st October 1975. All persons leaving the UDR, for whatever reason, are formally discharged and the latter figure includes 84 members who tendered their resignation before completion of their engagements.

Mr. R. C. Mitchell asked the Secretary of State for Defence what orders his Department expects to place for the Harrier Carrier and the Seawolf armed broad-beam Type 21 frigate; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. William Rodgers: We have no plans to order either of these ships the first of which is only at the conceptual stage. They are private ventures designed primarily for export.

Mr. Urwin asked the Secretary of State for Defence what representations he has received from trade unions and other organisations about job losses arising from
467 the review of defence expenditure; what discussions he has undertaken: and if he will make a statement.

Mr. William Rodgers: Representations from trade unions, especially in the aircraft and guided weapons, industries, have continued since my right hon. Friend's statement of 3rd December 1974. I met a further deputation representing Hawker Siddeley Dynamics as recently as Friday last. As for civilians employed by the Ministry of Defence, consultations have already begun in order to achieve the savings set out in the Defence White Paper. Ministers continue to make clear on all suitable occasions that cuts in defence spending must inevitably be reflected in a loss of job opportunities.
Mr. Urwin asked the Secretary of State for Defence if he will make a statement about the future of the defence equipment industries.

Mr. William Rodgers: The defence industries have a long record in the development and production of high quality equipment. Our Services will have a continuing need for their support within the limits set by the level of defence expenditure. The industries will also have their part to play in our endeavours to increase standardisation and to extend the scope of collaboration and joint procurement which is essential if the NATO Alliance is to obtain the maximum military benefit from defence resources. In addition their export contribution will remain very important.

Mr. Urwin asked the Secretary of State for Defence what discussions he has had with Scandinavian countries concerning stockpiling of military equipment and provision of training facilities within the terms of NATO.
Mr. William Rodgers: The logistic support and training arrangements for forces earmarked for the reinforcement of AFNORTH are discussed regularly both in NATO fora and bilaterally with host nations.
Mr. Hardy asked the Secretary of State for Defence if he is satisfied with the arrangements for the air defence of the United Kingdom.

Mr. John: Yes. The air defence of the United Kingdom is undertaken by well-equipped forces which are kept up to date and effective. The programme of building hardened shelters for RAF aircraft in Germany is now nearly completed and we are putting in hand a similar programme at RAF bases in the United Kingdom. In addition, a number of Bloodhound surface-to-air missiles, which have become available from withdrawals from overseas, will be deplored in eastern England to supplement our air defences and a number of Rapier missiles will shortly be deployed in Scotland. These measures, together with the replacement of the Shackleton AEW aircraft and improvements in the ground-based warning and control systems planned over the next few years, reflect the priority given in the Defence Review to the security of the United Kingdom bases.

Mr. Trotter asked the Secretary of State for Defence with the navy of which friendly countries (a) in CENTO and (b) otherwise, exercises have taken place aimed at ensuring the continued security of oil traffic from the Gulf to the United Kingdom following the development by the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics of a naval base at Somalia.
Mr. Judd: I have nothing to add to my reply to the hon. Member on 30th October.—[Vol. 898, c. 582.]

Dr. Reginald Bennett asked the Secretary of State for Defence what is the total civilian labour force employed at, and in connection with HMS "Daedalus" and other naval establishments at Lee-on-Solent.

Mr. Judd: Seven hundred and sixty-nine Ministry of Defence and Department of the Environment civilians are employed at HMS "Daedalus". A further 56 civilians work there for NAAFI and other organisations.

Mr. David Howell asked the Minister for the Civil Service what is the number of vacancies in Government Departments
469 and subordinate agencies for which recruits are required but which have not yet been filled.
Mr. Charles R. Morris: This information is not available centrally since the greater part of recruitment is carried out by Government Departments under delegated arrangements.
Mr. Hordern asked the Minister for the Civil Service what was the total wage and salary bill of non-industrial and industrial staff in post on 1st July 1975 and 1st March 1974.

Mr. Charles R. Morris: Information is not available in the form specified and figures could not be calculated without disproportionate effort. The provision in the Supply Estimates for all United Kingdom based civil servants for the financial years ending 31st March has been as follows:
Estimates £m.
1973–74 1,509
1974–75 1,840
1975–76 2,252
The figure for 1975–76 includes Summer Supplementary Estimates only.
Mr. Aitken asked the Minister for the Civil Service if he has any plans to include Thanet in the deployment of Civil Service jobs.

Mr. Charles R. Morris: There are at present no plans to disperse Civil Service work to Thanet. In any future plans for dispersal from London or the setting up of new offices priority will be given where-ever possible to the assisted areas. However, the interests of other areas will also be taken into account before decisions are made.

Mr. Michael Latham asked the Minister for the Civil Service to what legislative or policy factors he attributes the increase in the non-industrial staff in the Civil Service Department from 3,492 on 1st March 1974 to 3,779 on 1st July 1975.

Mr. Charles R. Morris: The increase has followed from additional central responsibilities in providing payroll and computer services, staff restaurant facilities and training for departments generally.

Mr. Lawson asked the Minister for the Civil Service whether retired civil servants, now resident abroad, receive inflation-proofed pension increases under the 1971 Act, or whether their pensions are frozen at the level obtaining at the time of their emigration, as is the case with State retirement pensions.
Mr. Charles R. Morris: Retired public servants receive increases under the provisions of the Pensions (Increase) Act 1971 wherever they reside.

Mr. Lawson asked the Minister for the Civil Service what will be the percentage increases in public service pensions, other than those paid to former civil servants, that come into force on 1st December; what will be the cost of this increase; and how many former public servants, other than civil servants, will be in receipt of pensions in excess of £8,500 following this increase.

Mr. Charles R. Morris: For all the public services directly covered by the Pensions (Increase) Act 1971 pensions which came into payment before 2nd July 1974, between 2nd July 1974 and 1st January 1975, and between 2nd January 1975 and 1st July 1975 will be increased on 1st December by 26·1 per cent., 29·3 per cent. and 19·9 per cent. respectively. Armed Forces pensions are increased on an analogous basis. The cost, excluding that in respect of Civil Service pensioners, is estimated to be some £142 million over the 12 months to December 1976.

A total of some 130 public service pensioners who served in the Armed Forces, the judiciary, the National Health Service and teaching will have pensions of £8,500 or more following the 1st December increase, service pensioners.
Information is not available centrally about local government, police or fire
Mr. Nicholas Winterton asked the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what instructions have been given to United Kingdom embassies to assist in enforcing anti-dumping legislation.

Mr. Ennals: None of a standing and general nature. Her Majesty's Missions overseas may be involved in particular cases to the extent that they provide confidential channels of diplomatic communication and information on matters of concern to Her Majesty's Government.

Mr. Cyril Smith asked the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs if he will publish in the Official Report the number of nations which have accepted the 1972 Collision Regulations and those nations which have so far not accepted those regulations.

Mr. Ennals: The Inter-Governmental Maritime Consultative Organisation is the depositary power for the Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972, and it is understood that the following States, in addition to the United Kingdom, have signed and ratified, accepted, approved or acceded to the Convention:
Brazil. Bulgaria, Canada. Denmark, France, German Democratic Republic, Ghana, Greece, Iceland, India, Liberia, Nigeria, Norway, Romania, Spain, Sweden, USSR.
The following States have signed the Convention, subject to ratification or acceptance:
Belgium, Cambodia, Federal Republic of Germany, Finland, Indonesia, Ireland, Italy, Kuwait, New Zealand, Poland, Portugal, Republic of Korea, Switzerland, USA.
It is understood that the following States have indicated an intention of acceding to the Regulations: Argentina, Israel, Pakistan, Syria.

Mr. Trotter asked the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs who is the accredited representative of the Maldivian Government in 472 London; and what is the address of the Maldivian Government offices in London.
Mr. Rowlands: The Republic of Maldives has no accredited representative to the United Kingdom, and there is no Maldivian Government office in London.

Mr. Geoffrey Finberg asked the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs on how many occasions in the 12 months ended 30th September 1975 he made public representations to overseas Governments in respect of sentences, trials, arrests, interrogation and alleged ill-treatment of foreign nationals; and which countries were the subject of such representations.

Mr. Ennals: During the 12 months in question my right hon. Friend has made representations, which have been made public at the time or subsequently, on one or other of the subjects listed above on some 18 occasions to the following countries: Chile, Ethiopia, Portugal, Rhodesia, South Africa and Spain.

Mr. Corbett asked the Secretary of State for Trade whether he will now have further discussions with the insurance industry to encourage them to take full responsibility for the claims of Nation Life policyholders.

Mr. Clinton Davis: There is no point in my entering into further discussions with the insurance industry, which has already made its position very clear. I am sure that the House will be pleased that the industry has implemented a scheme of rescue for the holders of conventional life policies issued by the company.

Mr. David Mitchell asked the Secretary of State for Trade when he intends to reply to the letter sent on 15th September by the managing director of an exporting company seeking his support for an export order; and when he will reply to the letter from the hon. Member for Basingstoke dated 10th October 1975 on the same subject.

Mr. Deakins: Oral advice on the question, about policy on trade, was conveyed by officials to the company before its director's negotiations in the country concerned. My right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for Trade has now confirmed that advice in a written reply.

Mr. Nicholas Winterton asked the Secretary of State for Trade what was the total cost of advertising by his Department in daily and Sunday national newspapers for each of the months March, April, May, June, July, August, September and October this year.

Mr. Deakins: The approximate total cost of such advertising placed either by the Department of Trade or by the Central Office of Information on its behalf for the period was as follows:
£
March 100
April 400
May —
June 300
July 100
August 350
September —
October 5,300

Mr. Michael McNair-Wilson asked the Secretary of State for Trade what discussions he has had with the British Airports Authority about modifying the take-off and landing procedures for Concorde at London Airport to enable the aircraft to create as little noise as possible.

Mr. Clinton Davis: There have been no such discussions because this is not a matter for which the British Airports Authority has responsibility. I would however refer the hon. Member to the reply given on 20th October—[Vol. 898, c. 147]—to the hon. Member for Windsor and Maidenhead (Dr. Glyn).

Mr. Grist asked the Secretary of State for Trade if he will list for each of the last three years the number of civil servants in his Department who have been prematurely retired on grounds of (i) inefficiency, (ii) limited efficiency, (iii) redundancy and (iv) discipline, showing executive and administrative grades separately.

Mr. Deakins: Since my Department was formed on 5th March 1974 only two officers in the Administration Group—Executive Officers and above—have been retired prematurely on any of the grounds indicated—both on grounds of limitced effiiency—one in 1974 and one in 1975.

Mr. Cyril Smith asked the Secretary of State for Trade how many airlines operating to and from the United Kingdom have conformed with the request of his Department issued on 30th October that retail commissions should be no more than 7½ per cent. of the applicable published air fares.
Mr. Clinton Davis: The 41 airlines that have replied so far have confirmed they are applying the approved commission rates.
Mr. Hoyle asked the Secretary of State for Trade what evidence he has that Japanese television tubes are being sold 15 per cent. cheaper in the United Kingdom than in Japan.

Mr. Deakins: None. As recently announced, an inquiry was carried out this year into alleged dumping of Japanese television tubes; no significant dumping was found. The Departments of Trade and of Industry will, however, be keeping a watch on imports through surveillance licensing to be introduced shortly.

Mr. Hoyle asked the Secretary of State for Trade why no agreement was reached with the Japanese Government not to continue the CENTO-limitation arrangement on television receivers; why shipments of Japanese colour television receivers have increased from an average of 9,500 per month, to 17,579 in August; and what action he is taking on this matter.

Mr. Deakins: Unilateral restraint on exports of colour television sets to the United Kingdom is a matter for the Japanese Government. Imports of Japanese colour television sets in the first nine months of 1975 were 40 per cent. below the figure for the same period in 1974. We have made it clear to the Japanese Government that we shall be ready to
475 use the powers at our disposal if there is a disruptive increase in imports of colour television sets. Meanwhile, we have announced our intention to introduce import surveillance licensing in 1976 to enable us to monitor trends more closely.

Mr. Cordle asked the Secretary of State for Trade whether he is now able to report some progress on his consultations with the shipping industry and other interested parties regarding the introduction of legislation to implement the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships, 1973.

Mr. Clinton Davis: The Department's studies both at the national level and the international level in IMCO have made good progress, but I am not yet in a position to say when legislation will be introduced. In the meantime, I note that progress is being made towards the general acceptance of the 1969 amendments to the 1954 Convention for the Prevention of Pollution of the Sea by Oil, 1954, which are substantially repeated in the 1973 Convention.

Mr. Adley asked the Secretary of State for Trade (1) if, pursuant to his answer on Concorde noise measurements on 13th October, when he stated that the figures in his answer were quoted in a unit of measurement, namely PNDB, not commonly used internationally for measurement and comparison of aircraft noise, he will now quote the figures in the internationally-used units of EPNDB, in order that comparisons with other aircraft can be made;

(2) if, pursuant to his answer on Concorde noise on 13th October, he will now give the comparable figures for noise, under similar conditions, in the unit commonly used internationally for measurement and comparison of aircraft noise, of Concorde, DC8-50 and Boeing 707/320C; and how many aircraft movements of each of these three types of aircraft he expects at Heathrow weekly in 1976.

Mr. Clinton Davis: Noise measurements are normally made in perceived noise decibels (PNdB) at Heathrow and at many other airports. The results of 476 this summer's Concorde endurance trials are not available in effective perceived noise decibels (EPNdB) and this information could only be obtained at disproportionate cost. However, I would refer the hon. Member to the reply given on 28th October—[Vol. 898, c. 417–18]—to the hon. Member for Thornaby (Mr. Wrigglesworth) by my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for Industry announcing the results of the Casablanca trials in EPNdB and giving comparative data for the Boeing 707 and DC8. When Concorde comes into commercial service at Heathrow it will not initially exceed four movements a week. The number of 707 and DC8 movements is not expected to be significantly different from those in 1975, about 550 and 200 per week respectively.

Mr. Adley asked the Secretary of State for Trade if, pursuant to his Answer on Concorde noise measurements on 13th October, when he gave the maximum take-off and landing readings at various mobile points, on given dates, he will now give the minimum noise measurements, at the same measurement points, on the same dates, in order that both maximum and minimum measurements may be compared, and an assessment made of the noise measurements of the aircraft.

Mr. Clinton Davis: The recorded noise of an aircraft rises from zero to a peak and falls back to zero as the aircraft passes a monitoring point. The figures quoted were the maximum levels recorded at the particular monitoring points.
Mr. Golding asked the Secretary of State for Trade what has been the level of telecommunication exchange equipment exports from Great Britain in each of the last 10 years.

Mr. Deakins: Following is the information for switchboards and exchanges:
