body.p: Mr. Hoyle asked the Secretary of State for Social Services what instructions have been given by her to regional and area health authorities to purchase British textiles.

Dr. Owen: Health authorities have been asked to ensure first that tenders for the supply of textiles require the country of origin to be stated, and secondly that when awarding contracts on a value for money basis these origins are considered together with quality, durability, speed and continuity of delivery, convenience of production inspections and quality control and the conditions under which the goods are produced.

Mr. Aitken asked the Secretary of State for Social Services how many patients discharged from mental hospital are currently being accommodated in the Thanet area; and how many of these are living in approved accommodation, run by qualified staff.

Dr. Owen: Comprehensive figures are not available. The Kent County Social Services Department is trying to make an accurate assessment of the numbers of such cases so that the matter can be examined further in collaboration with the health authorities.

Mr. Ridley asked the Secretary of State for Social Services what was the yield of prescription charges, and the average charge per prescription, in 1973–74; what are the figures for the current financial year; and what has been the decline in the value of the £ sterling in the same period.

Dr. Owen: Information in respect of prescriptions dispensed by chemists in England is as follows:
Yield of charges £ million Average charge per prescription (all prescriptions)
1973–74 22·9 8·7p
1975–76 (estimated) 22·8 8·1p
The decline in the internal purchasing power of the £ sterling between September 1973 and September 1975 was about 32 per cent., based on changes in the general index of retail prices.

Mr. Banks asked the Secretary of State for Social Services what are the scales of pay in the 16 to 21 years age range applicable to laboratory assistants in National Health Service hospitals; and when the present scales were fixed.

Dr. Owen: There is no nationally recognised grade of laboratory assistant in National Health Service hospitals, but laboratory assistants in the blood transfusion service aged 18 or over receive the adult rate of weekly paying ranging from £30·52 to £32·32 and at ages 16 and 17 receive respectively 70 per cent. and 85 per cent. of these rates.

Mr. William Hamilton asked the Secretary of State for Social Services how many administrative staff with medical qualifications are employed within her Department; and what were the comparable figures three years ago.

Mrs. Castle: In November 1975 the medical administrative staff of the Department of Health and Social Security in England included 340 qualified doctors, a number of whom devote a proportion of their time to duties of a clinical nature. The comparable figure for 1st November 1972 was 241 doctors.

Mr. Cartwright asked the Secretary of State for Social Services if, in order to reduce the demands on the National Health Service, she will give additional support to the promotion of better health education.

Dr. Owen: I attach considerable importance to health education and to the preventive services generally, and I am anxious to stimulate greater awareness of these matters among national health service and other authorities. The Department issued a comprehensive circular in March 1974 about the promotion of health education services in the reorganised National Health Service.

I have already announced my intention to publish a consultative document on preventive medicine early in the new year. This document, which will stress the importance of health education, among other preventive measures, will be
549 widely circulated among the health professions and members of the public interested in health matters including hon. Members, members of National Health Service and local authorities, and community health councils. Its aim will be broadly to inform and to provoke dis-National Health Service authorities to cussion. I hope that this will encourage give preventive medicine, including health education, greater priority when considering their future plans and in allocating resources.
In the meantime the Department will continue to give full support to the work of the Health Education Council.

Mr. Cartwright asked the Secretary of State for Social Services if she will bring forward proposals to give community health councils powers to conciliate in disputes between patients and their general practitioners which do not relate to the technical competence of the doctor.

Dr. Owen: I assume that my hon. Friend is referring to complaints which do not allege that a doctor has failed to comply with his terms of service and cannot, therefore, be dealt with formally under the service committee procedure. There is an agreed procedure operated by many family practitioner committees, under which a lay member of the service committee, with a medically qualified member to assist him, is appointed to deal informally with complaints against
ENGLAND
1970 1971 1972 1973 1974
Daily available hospital beds within the National Health Service 423,621 419,612 412,664 403,526 396,235
Total Administrative and Clerical Staff (See Note 1) 58,262 61,651 65,491 69,417 74,716

Notes.—1. Administrative and clerical staff within the purview of the National Health Service Administrative and Clerical Staffs Whitley Council. Figures exclude staff of the former local health authorities and ambulance officers who, prior to 1st April 1974, were not included in the National Health Service administrative and clerical group.

2. A significant additional staff work load, assumed by health authorities in 1974, was the central administration of community health services; in respect of these functions £8 million, mainly repre-

general practitioners in cases where, at any rate initially, it appears that a formal investigation may not be necessary or appropriate. Cases where there is no allegation of a breach of the terms of service may be dealt with under this procedure. Alternatively the complaint may be dealt with informally by the Family Practitioner Services Administrator.

In the Government's view, community health councils would not be appropriate bodies to deal with disputes between individual general practitioners and their patients. At the same time, I hope the family practitioner committees will work closely with the community health councils. The councils can be of great assistance in explaining to members of the public the operation of the services administered by the committees and by ensuring that individual patients' complaints, both formal and informal, are passed promptly to the FPS administrator. The councils can also help committees by advising them of public feeling on more general issues affecting the availability of practitioner services in each district.

Mr. William Hamilton asked the Secretary of State for Social Services if she will publish in the Official Report a table showing the total numbers of administrative staff within the NHS in each of the last five years; and the number of beds in hospitals in the same period.
Mr. Meacher: The following table shows the figures requested:
senting staff costs, for England as a whole was transferred to the NHS from Local Authorities with no corresponding transfer of staff.
3. Staff figures are whole time equivalents.

Mr. Evelyn King asked the Secretary of State for Social Services how many administrators without medical qualifications within the health and hospital services or employed in her Department in connection with those services draw salaries in excess of £5,000, £7,000 and
551 £10,000, respectively; and what is the total of persons so employed.
Mr. Meacher: I will let the hon. Member have a reply as soon as possible.

Mr. Sedgmore asked the Secretary of State for Social Services what is the number of families in owner-occupied property who are currently in receipt of supplementary benefit; and what percentage of beneficiaries these figures represent.
Mr. O'Malley: About 390,000 claimants representing 13·6 per cent. of all beneficiaries.

Mr. Christopher Price asked the Secretary of State for Social Services how many tuberculosis visitors there were in post without health visitor certificates on 1st May 1974, and how many there were on 1st November 1975.

Mr. Meacher: The number of tuberculosis visitors without health visitor certificates in the NHS is not collected separately from those with the certificate. On 1st April 1974 the number of all NHS tuberculosis visitors in England was 146, and on 30th September 1974, the latest date for which figures are available, is provisionally estimated to have been 147 in whole-time equivalents.
Mr. Christopher Price asked the Secretary of State for Social Services if she will list the figures for the incidence of tuberculosis in 1973, 1974 and for the first half of 1975.

Dr. Owen: I indicated in my reply to the hon. Member for Chertsey and Walton (Mr. Pattie) on 16th October—[Vol. 897, c. 771.]—the numbers of notifications during the period 1964–1974. The number of cases notified in 1973 was 11,180 (corrected) and in 1974 10,687 (provisional). For the first six months of the current year the provisional figure is 5,699.
Mr. Thorpe asked the Secretary of State for Social Services how many different benefits are paid out of the National Insurance Fund; and how many are not available to the self-employed.

Mr. O'Malley: The following benefits, as referred to in Sections 12,38 and 50 of the Social Security Act 1975, in Section 36 of the National Insurance Act 1965 as preserved by transitional regulations, and in the Industrial Injuries and Diseases (Old Cases) Act 1975, are paid wholly or partly out of the National Insurance Fund:
Unemployment benefit.
Sickness benefit.
Invalidity benefit.
Maternity benefit.
Widow's benefit.
Retirement pension.
Child's special allowance.
Death Grant.
Guardian's allowance.
Graduated retirement benefit.
Injury benefit.
Disablement benefit.
Industrial death benefit.
Workmen's Compensation Supplementation.
Industrial Diseases Benefit in respect of pre-1948 employment.

Those not available to the self-employed are:
Unemployment benefit (including earnings-related supplement).
Earnings-related supplement to sickness benefit.
Earnings-related supplement to maternity allowance.
Earnings-related addition to widow's allowance.
Graduated retirement benefit.
Injury benefit.
Disablement benefit.
Industrial death benefit.
Workmen's Compensation Supplementation.
Industrial Diseases Benefit in respect of pre-1948 employment.

The last five of the above list were covered by the broad description "industrial injuries benefits" in the reply given to my hon. Friend the Member for Islington, South and Finsbury (Mr. Cunningham) on 22nd January—[Vol. 884, c. 394–6]. Earnings-related supplement to maternity allowance was introduced in April 1975, after that reply was given. Special hardship allowance, to which the right hon. Gentleman referred in the debate on the self-employed, is not a separate benefit but is, like a number of other allowances, an increase in the rate of industrial disablement benefit.

The above lists of benefits follow in general the classification of benefits in the relevant statutes, and do not pay regard to subdivisions of the main benefits; for example, maternity allowance and the earnings-related supplement to it are included in maternity benefit, and
553 widow's allowance and the earnings-related addition to it are included in widow's benefit; in the second of the above lists however it has been necessary to depart from this classification for those benefits which are only partially available to the self-employed.

Mr. Rippon asked the Secretary of State for Social Services if she will take steps to relieve the hardship caused to patients in the widespread rural constituency of Hexham who are on or near supplementary benefit level but cannot receive travelling expenses to health services, outdoor clinics, health centres and hospitals; and what reply she has sent to the representations made by the Northumberland Community Health Council on this subject.

Dr. Owen: I have advised the Northumberland Community Health Council that help with travelling expenses can only be considered for those hospital patients who would suffer financial hardship as assessed by supplementary benefit standards. Although I have no plans to extend the scope of this scheme, some patients who at present are excluded may qualify for help when the rates of supplementary benefits are increased on 17th November.
Mrs. Millie Miller asked the Secretary of State for Social Services if she will announce the membership of the Committee on the Review of Medicines.

Dr. David Owen: Yes. My right hon. Friend the Secretary of State and my right hon. Friends the Secretaries of State for Scotland and Wales and Northern Ireland have appinted the following as members of the Committee:
Sir Erick Scowen, MD, DSc, FRCP, FRCS, FRCP Ed, FRC Path, Emeritus Professor of Medicine, St. Bartholomew's Hospital.
Dr. T. B. Binns, FRCP, DCH, Department of Pharmacology and Therapeutics, London Hospital Medical College.
J. C. Bloomfield, Esq., OBE, FPS, FBOA, General practice pharmacist.
Professor P. Curzen, BSc, MD, FRCOG, Professor of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Westminster Medical School, University of London.
Dr. D. G. Davey, OBE, MSc, PhD, F Inst Biol, Research director in Pharmaceutical Industry (retired).
Dr. José Day, MB, MRCGP, General practitioner, London.
Dr. D. C. Garratt, DSc, PhD, MPS. M Chem A, RIC, Scienific Adviser to the Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain.
Professor M. R. P. Hall, BM, BCh, FRCP, FRCP(Ed), Professor of Geriatric Medicine, Southampton University.
Dr. F. Dudley Hart, MD, FRCP, Consultant Physician, Westminster Hospital, London.
Sir A. Bradford Hill, CBE, PhD, DSc, FRS, Emeritus Professor of Medical Statistics. University of London.
W. G. Hollis, Esq., FPS, Former director, Proprietary Association of Great Britain.
Dr. Catharine E. Hollman, MB, BS, DPH, MFCM, Area Medical Officer, Hillingdon Area Health Authority.
Dr. M. H. Lader, MD, PhD, DPM. MRC Psych, Reader in Clinical Psychopharmacology, University of London.
Professor W. Linford Rees, PRC Psych, MD, FRCP, DPM, Professor of Psychiatry, University of London and St. Bartholomew's Hospital, London.
Dr. J. R. Newton, MD, MRCOG, Senior Lecturer/Consultant Gynaecologist, King's College Hospital, London.
Professor F. W. O'Grady, TD, MD, MSc, FRC Path, Professor of Microbiology, University of Nottingham.
Dr. D. Ritchie, PhD, ARIC, MPS, Quality control manager in pharmaceutical industry (retired).
Professor R. W. Smithells, MB, FRCP, FRCP(Ed), Professor in Paediatrics and Child Health, University of Leeds.
Professor W. Walker, MA, MB, FRCP, FRCP(Ed), Regius Professor of Materia Medica, Department of Therapeutics and Clinical Pharmacology, University of Aberdeen.
Dr. G. Watkinson, MD, BS, FRCP, FRCP(GIas), Consultant Physician and Gastro-Enterologist, Western Infirmary, Gartnavel General Hospital and Southern General Hospital, Glasgow.
Dr. W. O. Williams, OBE, BSc, MD, FRCGP, General Practitioner and Honorary Director of the Swansea Research Unit of the Royal Colege of Genertal Practitioners.
Mr. Frank Allaun asked the Secretary of State for Social Services how many nurses were unemployed at the most recent date for which figures are available.
Mr. John Fraser: I have been asked to reply.

On 8th September 1975, 1,685 unemployed State registered and State enrolled nurses and State certified midwives and 1,468 unemployed nursing auxiliaries and assistants were registered at employment offices in Great Britain.
555 Information about the numbers of unemployed nurses is available from the occupational analysis of the unemployed which is compiled quarterly.

Mr. Michael McGuire asked the Secretary of State for Social Services if she will seek to amend the National Insurance (Industrial Injuries) (Amendment) Act 1967, so as to provide that anyone who is receiving a disablement pension 556 in respect of pneumoconiosis, even if it is less than 50 per cent., will be entitled to have his disability pension increased in respect of any assessable amount of bronchitis or emphysema.

Mr. O'Malley: No. The Industrial Injuries Advisory Council in its report on pneumoconiosis and byssinosis published two years ago examined the 50 per cent. rule and recommended that the provision should continue in its present form.

11. Mr. Jessel asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science how much his Department spent, through local authorities, on nursery education in the last financial year; and if he will give estimates for the current year, and for 1975–76.

Miss Joan Lestor: Recurrent expenditure by local education authorities on nursery education in England in the financial years 1974–75 and 1975–76 is estimated at £30 million and £35 million respectively, at 1975 survey prices.

34. Mrs. Renée Short asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science whether additional resources will be made available for the expansion of nursery education during 1976–77 in order to meet the needs of the pre-school child.
Miss Joan Lestor: A nursery education building programme of £8·5 million for starts in 1976–77 was announced in August.
23. Mr. Raphael Tuck asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science what effect the proposed cuts on education expenditure are likely to have on the teacher-pupil ratio in schools.
Mr. Mulley: The rate support grant settlement for 1976–77 is still being negotiated; but I expect that provision will be made to maintain present pupil-teacher ratios.
25. Mr. Hannam asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science what estimate he has made of the total of financial assistance given to the arts by industrial sponsorship.
Mr. Hugh Jenkins: I hope that more detailed and accurate estimates than those hitherto given will become possible following the discussions that are taking place.
42. Mr. Moonman asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science what 558 plans he has to ensure that local authorities make a full contribution to the availability of arts in the community.

Mr. Hugh Jenkins: It is for local authorities themselves to decide what contribution they should make to the availability of the arts, within the resources at their disposal. Government assistance is provided in various ways through the Arts Council, including grants to regional arts associations, the British Film Institute, the Area Museums Service and the acquisition funds administered by the Victoria and Albert and Science Museums.
16. Mr. Hooley asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science what is his policy on student representation on the governing bodies of colleges of education and polytechnics.
Mr. Mulley: I welcome the participation of students on governing bodies. When considering new instruments and articles of government I expect to see appropriate student representation.

40. Mr. John H. Osborn asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will set out a table in the Official Report showing the number of students and undergraduates in each of the main faculties, respectively, and in total in British universities, expressing these numbers as a percentage of the total number of university students, and, comparing the position with 1970 and 1965, whilst indicating his latest estimate of future trends.

Mr. Mulley: The following table shows for undergraduates and for all students, undergraduates and postgraduates, the numbers and percentages on full-time and sandwich courses in each of the main subject groups in British universities. 1973–74 is the latest year for which full information is available; for all subjects the 1974–75 totals are provisionally estimated at 251,000 students, of whom 204,000 were undergraduates. For future trends I would refer the hon. Member to the answer I gave to the hon. Member for the Isle of Ely (Mr. Freud) on 20th October 1975.—[Vol. 898, c. 73].

tr.td: Architecture and other professional and vocational subjects

body.p: 26. Mr. Madel asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science what plans he has to pay an official visit to schools in Bedfordshire.
Mr. Mulley: I have no plans to do so.
27. Mr. Michael McNair-Wilson asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science whether he is satisfied with the liaison between his Department and county education authorities.
Mr. Mulley: Yes.
28. Mr. Peter Morrison asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science what is his present estimate of the cost of the transition of all secondary schools into comprehensive.

Mr. Mulley: Many different forms of comprehensive organisation are possible, and, while making the fullest use of existing facilities, local education authorities have discretion as to the pattern they adopt. It is, therefore, not possible to provide an estimate of cost of the kind requested.

20. Mr. George Gardiner asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science whether he is satisfied with the operation of the system of limits to the catchment areas of schools within local education authorities.

Miss Joan Lestor: The designation of catchment areas for particular schools is a common, and normally satisfactory, means used by local education authorities for giving preference to certain applicants when the school cannot admit all of them.
24. Mr. Gould asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science what effort is being made to recognise the differing rates of growth in the school population in different parts of the country.

Miss Joan Lestor: Every effort is made to take account of expected instances of school population growth when the capital resources available to meet basic need for additional school places are distributed 562 between local education authorities by my right hon. Friend. It is for each authority to decide how best to use its allocation to meet the needs of individual localities within its area.

22. Mr. Sims asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science what representations he has received in respect of his proposals to close certain teacher training colleges; and what amendments he intends to make in the light of them.

Mr. Mulley: Almost every proposal that a college of education should cease initial training has met with objections. Such objections were carefully considered before final decisions were taken, and accordingly I have no plans to make amendments.
41. Mr. Hatton asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science how many places are at present available in teacher training colleges; and what is the percentage reduction planned by 1981.
Mr. Mulley: The number of teacher training places is being reduced by some 46 per cent. from about 114,000 to about 60,000 by 1981.

29. Mr. Kilroy-Silk asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on the progress of the discussions he is having with local authorities about the reintroduction of free schoolmilk for children aged 7 to 11 years.

Mr. Mulley: As I made clear in my answer to the hon. Member on 14th October—[Vol. 897, c. 1109–10.]—it is not possible in the present economic situation to reimpose the obligation to supply free school milk to all children of junior school age, and this possibility is not under discussion with the local authority associations.
30. Mr. Loyden asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science how many children over the age of 5 years do not receive full-time education.

Miss Joan Lestor: The precise number at any time is not known, but since
563 there is a general duty on parents, enforceable by local education authorities, to ensure that their children between 5 and 16 receive full-time education in school or otherwise, and exceptions to this are permitted only in extraordinary circumstances, it must be very small indeed.
31. Mr. Brittan asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science whether he has any plans to seek to amend the regulations for scholarships and other benefits.
Mr. Mulley: I am considering legislation which will among other things permit me to review the exercise by LEAs of certain powers conferred on them by these regulations.
32. Mrs. Bain asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he is satisfied that current Government expenditure on universities is adequate.

Mr. Mulley: I realise that the universities, in common with other sectors of education, have had to bear severe economies, and that the need for economy will continue. In the present financial situation I consider that the grant of £465 million for recurrent expenditure in the academic year 1975–76 is a reasonable settlement.

33. Dr. Boyson asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will set up an independent inquiry to collect, publish and comment on the academic results in local authorities before and after comprehensive reorganisation.

Mr. Mulley: No. I do not think that such a comparison would be helpful, since the academic results of pupils are affected by the whole of their education, not merely by the type of school they are attending when they sit a public examination.
35. Dr. Hampson asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science what responsibilities his Department has for approving degree courses in reorganised colleges of education.

Mr. Mulley: Under Regulation 8 of the Further Education Regulations 1975, which apply to all establishments of further education, including colleges providing courses of teacher training, the provision of any full-time or part-time course of study in preparation for a degree requires my Department's approval.

Mr. Edge asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will publish in the Official Report the estimated number of teachers completing training for each year from 1970 to 1980 and the estimated number of teacher job vacancies for each year during the same period.

Mr. Mulley: The numbers of students successfully completing courses of initial training in England and Wales are estimated to be:
1970 38,200
1971 40,400
1972 42,000
1973 42,000
1974 41,400
1975 39,800
1976 37,300
1977 34,800
1978 33,300
1979 28,000
No estimate can usefully be made for 1980 until the number to be admitted to courses in September 1977 has been decided.
No estimates are available of vacancies, since they arise partly from wastage from the profession and partly from movement of teachers between schools.
36. Mr. Graham asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement about the problem of stocks of nitrate-based film at the National Film Archive.

Mr. Hugh Jenkins: The Health and Safety Executive will shortly complete a series of investigations into the safety of the storage of nitrate films at the National Film Archive, which I shall be visiting in the near future. I am advised that there is no immediate cause for alarm, but some facilities at the Archive have had to be restricted; additional temporary and permanent storage has recently ended the overstocking of the storage vaults. When the Health and Safety Executive has reported, the British
565 Film Institute, which is responsible for the Archive, will no doubt wish to discuss any necessary action with me. A further problem at the Archive is that of conserving the nitrate film and transferring it to stable film. I am anxious that this work should progress as fast as resources permit.

Mr. Mulley: Local education authorities are not required to give me details of their budgets. The aggregate level of education expenditure in 1976–77 is under discussion between the Government and the local authorities' associations in preparation for the rate support grant settlement for 1976–77.
38. Mr. Rooker asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on the progress made towards implementation of the Vernon Report.
Mr. Litterick asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science what steps he is taking to implement the recommendations of the Vernon Report on the education of visually handicapped children.

Miss Joan Lestor: Many of the report's recommendations are addressed to the local education authorities or the schools. The most far-reaching recommendation was for plans to be made for the distribution, organisation and management of special schools and other educational services for the visually handicapped; and I hope that moves in this direction will result from the regional conferences promoted by my Department this year at which LEAs have been invited to review, with the voluntary bodies concerned, the needs of all types of handicap, including visual, within their region.

My right hon. Friend's predecessor announced in June 1974 his acceptance of the recommendation that in future it 566 should be a requirement for teachers of the partially sighted to obtain an additional specialist qualification after obtaining qualified teacher status. The number of full-time training places for teachers of visually handicapped has been increased this September from 14 to 20, and discussions are continuing on the provision of a new part-time course of training.
Mr. Edge asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will seek powers to abolish selective secondary education for blind and partially sighted children.

39. Mr. Litterick asked the Secretary of State for Education and Science what steps he is taking to abolish the use of the principle of selective entry to secondary education for visually handicapped children.

Miss Joan Lestor: Because of the small numbers of children involved and the highly specialised facilities and skills required for teaching certain subjects, the reasons for abolishing selection which apply to non-handicapped children do not necessarily apply to the handicapped. Exhall Grange School in Warwickshire, however, already takes partially sighted children with a wide range of ability, with a national intake for academic courses and a regional intake for other courses. We are discussing with the Royal National Institute for the Blind the future of their two grammar schools for the blind, including ways in which the ability range of the scholars might be widened, as at Exhall Grange.

executive and administrative grades separately.

Friend for confirmation its proposals to obtain increased revenue without which it considers that it would not be possible to maintain an adequate fisheries programme for the future. 577 legislation on agricultural holdings he proposes to introduce, announced in a reply to the hon. Member for Brecon and Radnor (Mr. Roderick) on 3rd November, will be designed to afford to the sons and near relatives of tenant farmers a status comparable to that which they enjoy in Scotland.

Mr. Strang: Discussions on this subject were held earlier this year with representatives of the agricultural industry and the interested professional bodies. Mr. Cope asked the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what measures proposed by the Forestry Commission to increase the outlets for elm timber have been approved by Ministers.

Mr. Strang: The Forestry Commission is actively pursuing consultations with the timber trade, Government Departments and nationalised industries, aimed at increasing the market for elm through encouraging its substitution for other timber. In conjunction with the Princes Risborough Laboratory of the Department of the Environment, a new publication is in preparation to draw attention to the possible uses of this high quality native hardwood. The commission is also making available on request local advice on marketing and storage, including possible storage sites on commission land.

Mr. Watt asked the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if he will take steps to simplify the conditions of the Farm and Horticulture Development Scheme, EEC Directive 159; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Strang: Measures to simplify the Farm and Horticulture Development Scheme are under consideration. We hope to present the necessary legislation to Parliament early in the new year.

Mr. Trotter asked the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food whether in 578 considering the level of future aid to the fishing industry, he will take into account the additional costs incurred by the industry in survey fees, alterations, new equipment, additional slippage and loss of fishing time as a result of the Safety Provisions Rules 1975; and what is his estimate of the likely additional costs in each of the next five years.

Mr. Bishop: Full account is taken of all the economic factors when considering the need for aid. Wherever possible safety surveys requiring inspection of the vessel out of the water will be combined with the need for the vessel to be slipped, when it will be for operational reasons. On this basis remedial works, if any, will frequently be inseparable from those for improvement and maintenance. It is impracticable to forecast such costs on an industry-wide basis.

Mr. Warren asked the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what consideration he is giving to the publication of a White Paper on the United Kingdom fishing policy.

Current research projects are directed towards the use of residues as a raw material for industrial products of relatively high value rather than as a fuel for which wood has a relatively low value.

Mr. Grimond asked the Secretary of State for Energy if he has any estimates of the comparative size of the energy reserves in oil, coal and gas in England, 582 Wales and Scotland, respectively, including the areas of the North Sea presumed appropriate to these countries.

Mr. Benn: Figures for oil and gas have previously been published in the 1975 Brown Book which show from presently designated areas that "proven", "probable" and "possible" reserves in existing licences total 3,100 million tons of oil—5,270 mtce—and 45 trillion cu. ft. of gas—1,640 mtce. It is well known that the majority of oil reserves have been discovered in waters to the North East of the British Isles and 60 per cent. of free gas reserves in the Southern Gas (Geological) Basin with 40 per cent. free gas and associated gas in the Northern (Geological) Basin. The latest estimate of the total known amount of United Kingdom coal reserves in place as reported to the World Energy Conference is about 97,300 million tons of which about 11,700 million is in Scotland, 24,700 million in Wales and 60,900 million in England. The corresponding estimate of economically recoverable coal reserves currently accessible to existing mines and extensions to existing mines is about 3,800 million tons of which about 3,160 million is in England, 290 million in Scotland and 350 million in Wales. In addition, there are further substantial recoverable reserves which can become accessible in the future both at existing and possible new pits.
Because of the differences in classification of coal reserves compared with those for oil and gas, it is not possible to compare categories directly.

Mr. Tom King asked the Secretary of State for Industry how many vacancies in his Department there are for which recruits are required but which have not yet been filled.
Mr. Kaufman: Recruits are currently required for 58 of the vacancies in the approved staffing establishment for my Department to 1st April next.

Mr. Tom King asked the Secretary of State for Industry how many staff were employed by his Department in March 1974; how many are currently employed; and what increase if any he expects for the rest of 1975 and 1976.

Mr. Kaufman: On 1st October 1975, the most recent date for which details are available, there were 10,209 staff in post. On 31st March 1974 the corresponding number, adjusted for subsequent machinery of Government changes, was 9,723. Supply Estimates for 1975–76 allow for up to 10,488 staff by 31st March 1976. A further small increase may be needed during the remainder of 1976, primarily for new work arising from the Industry Bill.

Mr. Tom King asked the Secretary of State for Industry for what reasons any extra staff were recruited since March 1974; and for what reasons any extra staff will be recruited for the rest of 1975 and 1976.

Mr. Kaufman: Extra staff have been recruited since March 1974 mainly in order to replace secretarial assistance provided by agencies; to undertake extra work arising under the Industry Act 1972 and on research and development activity; to provide enhanced statistical services; and to fill hitherto existing vacancies mainly in personnel management work. The main reasons for the expected recruitment of additional staff during the rest of 1975 and 1976 are for new work arising from the Industry Bill and for security of buildings occupied by the Department.

Mr. Tom King asked the Secretary of State for Industry if he will transfer an official from his present duties in the Department with a view to seeking out possible areas where economies can be made in the Department's spending and for formulating plans for implementing economies.
Mr. Kaufman: No. Such a procedure would not be economical.
Mr. Tom King asked the Secretary of State for Industry what progress he has made in studying his Department's estimates with a view to making economies.

Mr. Kaufman: Consideration of possible economies is a continuing aspect of the management of public expenditure programmes. All programmes are reviewed as part of the annual public expenditure survey, and the outcome of the 1975 survey will be reflected in the Public Expenditure White Paper.
Mr. Tebbit asked the Secretary of State for Industry if the financial control mechanism of his Department includes forecast spending levels through the year.
Mr. Gregor Mackenzie: Yes.

Mr. Tebbit asked the Secretary of State for Industry if he has adequate means of monitoring whether the spending of his Department is currently running above or below the level envisaged in the estimates upon which the Chancellor's Budget was based.
Mr. Gregor Mackenzie: Yes.

Mr. Tebbit asked the Secretary of State for Industry whether the spending of his Department is currently running above or below the level envisaged when he made his expenditure estimates upon which the Chancellor's Budget is based.

Mr. Kaufman: Since the Budget a number of policy decisions have been taken which will lead to increased expenditure, of which the most important are the purchase of shares in BLMC and the schemes for additional support to industry under Section 8 of the Industry Act 1972 announced in the Budget itself and since extended. Additional expenditure will also be required for support for certain individual firms under Sections 7 and 8 of the Industry Act; these have been the subject of separate announcements. Provision for BLMC, for payments under the Statutory Corporations (Financial Provisions) Act and for provision of additional public dividend capital to the British Steel Corporation, was taken in the 1975–76 Summer Supplementary Estimates. Provision for the remaining new expenditures referred to will be sought in the Winter Supplementaries.

Mr. Warren asked the Secretary of State for Industry what steps are being taken, in collaboration with the British Steel Corporation, to help find jobs for the 40,000 workers who will lose their jobs in the steel industry under the plan agreed between the British Steel Corporation and Her Majesty's Government.

Mr. Kaufman: The Government are doing everything possible to attract new industry in the steel closure areas, including the maximum use of selective financial assistance under the Industry Act 1972 and the provision of Government factories. In addition, the British Steel Corporation has been encouraged to participate in new ventures there.
Mr. Corrie asked the Secretary of State for Industry what proportion of the Regional Development Fund has been allocated to Scotland.
Mr. Gregor Mackenzie: The Fund Regulations established a share of the fund for the United Kingdom, but no subdivision within it.

Mr. Nicholas Winterton asked the Secretary of State for Industry what was the total cost of advertising by his Department in daily and Sunday national newspapers for each of the months March, April, May, June, July, August, September and October this year.

Mr. Gregor Mackenzie: The approximate total cost of such advertising placed either by the Department of Industry or by the Central Office of Information on its behalf was as follows:
£
March 59,600
April 35,700
May 46,000
June 47,800
July 34,500
August 3,600
September 23,700
October 35,600

Mr. Michael McNair-Wilson asked the Secretary of State for Industry whether the pilots of the Concorde aircraft used during the trial flights from London Airport in the summer were carrying out the full noise control enforcement procedures at all times.
Mr. Kaufman: I am advised that the pilots initiated noise abatement techniques on all flights, but that because of their experimental nature these were not given absolute priority.

Mr. Jim Spicer asked the Secretary of State for Industry what up to date information he has received from the boat building industry on the effects of the 25 per cent. VAT rate on the boat building industry of the United Kingdom.

Mr. Kaufman: My right hon. and noble Friend the Minister of State has recently received a letter from the Ship and Boat Building National Federation enclosing the results of a survey among its members relating to weekly orders received, monthly inquiries and employment in May and June 1975. The survey suggests that there has been a substantial drop in boat building activity compared with the same period last year, but it is not possible to evaluate with any accuracy the effect of the higher rate of VAT.

Mr. Jim Spicer asked the Secretary of State for Industry if he is now in possession of further information from the caravan industry on the effects on that industry of the 25 per cent. VAT rate on caravans.
Mr. Kaufman: The National Caravan Council has been asked to provide information on the effects on the caravan manufacturing industry of a higher rate of VAT. The council's reply is awaited.
Mr. Jim Lester asked the Secretary of State for Industry whether there has been any change in industrial development certificate policy for the Greater Nottingham area.
Mr. Gregor Mackenzie: No. The control continues to be operated with due regard to the circumstances of applicants and the needs and resources of individual localities.
Mr. Tebbit asked the Secretary of State for Industry if he will make a statement on the progress made in giving assistance to Ferranti Limited.

Mr. Kaufman: Following the statement made by my right hon. Friend the then Secretary of State for Industry on 14th May about the Heads of Agreement negotiated with Ferranti Limited a formal agreement was ratified by the company at a general meeting on 10th September. £15 million was paid to the company that day in respect of new equity and a loan.
Mr. Joseph Dean asked the Secretary of State for Industry whether he intends to set a time limit for the acceptance of applications for regional development grants.

Mr. Gregor Mackenzie: Yes. Under Section 5(1) of Part I of the Industry Act 1972 the Secretary of State may direct the time within which applications for grant shall be made, and it is intended that no grant shall be made on assets provided before 1st April 1974 unless an application is received by the Department on the appropriate form not later than 1st July 592 1976. For the period beginning 1st April 1974 and ending on 31st March 1975 applications should be received by 1st April 1977. Thereafter until further notice applications should be made not later than the end of two years after the end of the quarter during which the asset was provided. It is considered that this period strikes a fair balance between the need to give an applicant reasonably adequate time in which to present his application and the need to give the Department an adequate period in which to satisfy itself that the conditions and purposes of the Act have been observed. Exceptionally, if the Secretary of State is satisfied that the application is delayed for reasons beyond the control of the applicant consideration will be given to whether the late application may be accepted.

Mr. Trotter asked the Secretary of State for Industry how many overdrafts have been granted by the Giro; how many have had overdrawn balances in excess of £1,000; under what circumstances overdrafts in general and in excess of £1,000 in particular are granted; and how many debts have proved to be bad.

Mr. Gregor Mackenzie: Giro does not at present provide overdraft facilities. I do not have any details of the number of overdrawn accounts or bad debts, but the Post Office advises me that where overdrawing has occurred due to misjudgment or oversight, it sometimes exercises discretion in individual cases for short periods.

Mr. Rooker asked the Secretary of State for Industry if he is yet able to make a statement on the report of the United Kingdom zip fastener manufacturers' association relating to foreign imports which was sent to his Department on 22nd January 1975.

Mr. Kaufman: Discussions have recently been held with YKK Fasteners (UK) Ltd. about the levels of its imports from Japan and about its future operations in the United Kingdom. My right hon. and noble Friend the Minister for State hopes to reply soon to my hon. Friend the Member for Birmingham, Perry Barr (Mr. Rooker) and others who have written to him on this subject.
43. Mr. Bryant Godman Irvine asked the Secretary of State for Defence what increases a petty officer retiring from the Royal Navy in 1962 on a long-service pension of £4 4s. 4d. (£4·22) has received.
Mr. Judd: If he is 55 or over, the increases would be £4·70 making a total pension of £8·92.

Mr. Grist asked the Secretary of State for Defence if he will list for each of the last three years the number of civilian civil servants in his Department who have been prematurely retired on grounds of (i) inefficiency, (ii) limited efficiency, (iii) redundancy and (iv) discipline, showing executive and administrative grades separately.

Mr. William Rodgers: The information which relates to staff in the Administrative Group—executive officer and above—is as follows:
1973 1974 1975
1. Inefficiency Nil Nil Nil
2. Limited Efficiency 1 3 1
3. Redundancy 6 15 4
4. Discipline Nil Nil Nil
Mr. Watkinson asked the Secretary of State for Defence if he proposes an amnesty in the near future for long-term Army deserters; and, if so, to whom it would apply.
Mr. Robert C. Brown: I have no such proposal.
Mr. Watkinson asked the Secretary of State for Defence when there was last an amnesty for deserters; and to whom it applied.
Mr. Robert C. Brown: The last amnesty for deserters from Her Majesty's Forces was announced in 1953. It applied to those who deserted during the 1939–45 war.

Mr. Alexander Fletcher asked the Secretary of State for Defence if he will give a general direction to the Post Office to 594 provide a postal service for Service personnel at second-class postage rates.

Mr. William Rodgers: No. Forces postage rates are based on the principle that a service man should not incur greater postal costs by being posted overseas compared with being stationed in the United Kingdom. Present Forces concessionary rates are made possible by subsidies which we could not justify increasing at the present time.
Mr. Watkinson asked the Secretary of State for Defence what is the average sentence for an absentee or deserter of more than five years.
Mr. Robert C. Brown: This information is not readily available and could not be provided for any significant period without disproportionate effort.
Mr. Onslow asked the Secretary of State for Defence if he has received a formal request from the Egyptian Government for the purchase of Jaguar aircraft; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. William Rodgers: Information concerning sales of defence equipment to individual countries is confidential and has been so regarded by successive Governments.
Mr. Gwynfor Evans asked the Secretary of State for Defence what is the acreage of Welsh land used by the Armed Forces.

Mr. Robert C. Brown: As at 1st October 1975 the Ministry of Defence held 52,612 acres of freehold and leasehold land in Wales and 2,637 acres of foreshore. In addition, rights are held over a further 2,962 acres.
Mr. Gwynfor Evans asked the Secretary of State for Defence what is his latest estimate of the total cost of the MRCAs which the Government have ordered.
Mr. William Rodgers: No orders for production aircraft have yet been placed, and therefore I regret that I cannot give any estimate of total costs.

Mr. Wm. Ross asked the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland if he is aware that owners of businesses in Londonderry which have been bombed out or otherwise lost their premises as a result of terrorist activity are sometimes refused permission to rebuild on the site of the destroyed building and that such persons can only get market value for the destroyed building in such cases and not reinstatement value and that this can result in severe financial loss to the persons concerned; and if he will take steps to improve this situation.
Mr. Concannon: Some owners in Londonderry have been refused planning permission to reinstate bombed property because it is situated in an area due to be re-developed.

The Northern Ireland Department of Housing, Local Government and Planning is aware of the difficulty in which this may place property owners. The balance has to be struck between the wish to reinstate and the need for comprehensive

tr.td: AMOUNTS AND TYPES OF EXPLOSIVE MATERIAL IN LBS. RECOVERED FROM FINDS AND FROM NEUTRALISED DEVICES IN NORTHERN IRELAND

ol.li: 1. All except a few pounds of the commercial gelignite recovered was manufactured in the Republic of Ireland. Northern Ireland does not manufacture its own commercial explosive, however, and relies on supplies from the Irish Republic for its legal requirements.
2. The country of origin of the remaining three categories of explosive material recovered is not readily identifiable.

body.p: treatment to improve the whole city centre, but in the light of recent representations the Department is investigating the position in detail.

Where compensation for malicious damage to property is payable under the Criminal Injuries Acts, it is either determined by the court or, if determined by my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State, is subject to the applicant's right of appeal to the court. It is not intended that compensation should either enrich or impoverish the victim of damage.

Mr. Wm. Ross asked the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland if he will publish a list of the amounts and types of explosive material and detonators and their country of origin, which were recovered from terrorist organisations in Northern Ireland during the last 18 months ended 30 September 1975, and on a monthly basis.
Mr. Merlyn Rees, pursuant to his reply [Official Report, 15th October 1975; Vol. 897, c. 748], gave the following information:

tr.td: NUMBERS OF DETONATORS RECOVERED FROM FINDS AND FROM NEUTRALISED DEVICES IN NORTHERN IRELAND TOGETHER WITH THEIR COUNTRY OF ORIGIN

ol.li: (i) unidentifiable due to damage by controlled explosion or deterioration;
(ii) manufactured in Great Britain before 1971 for use in the Irish Republic or Northern Ireland and, therefore, unmarked;
(iii) manufactured in Great Britain for use in Great Britain and the rest of the world excluding the Irish Republic and Northern Ireland;
(iv) manufactured in countries other than Great Britain, America and Germany.

body.p: Mr. Hoyle asked the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland what advice has been given to Government and local authorities in Northern Ireland to purchase British textiles.

Mr. Merlyn Rees: No direction has been given to Government and local authorities in Northern Ireland on this subject. In practice, however, Government specifications for the purchase of textile goods provide that they must be to British standards. In addition, a 5 per cent. preference for goods manufactured in Northern Ireland applies to contracts awarded by Government Departments.
District councils in Northern Ireland have fewer functions than local authorities in Great Britain and accordingly the extent to which they purchase textiles is limited.

Mr. Grist asked the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland if he will list for each of the last three years the number of civil servants in his Department who 598 have been prematurely retired on grounds of (i) inefficiency, (ii) limited efficiency, (iii) redundancy and (iv) discipline, showing executive and administrative grades separately.
Mr. Merlyn Rees: No United Kingdom civil servants have been retired from the Northern Ireland Office on the grounds stated in the Question during the last three years.

Mr. Nicholas Winterton asked the Secretary of State for Prices and Consumer Protection what representations she has received about dangers created for young children by toy umbrellas imported from Hong Kong; and if she will make a statement.

Mr. Alan Williams: I have received the hon. Member's representations on behalf of a constituent about a toy umbrella. The information he has sent me does not indicate whether the toy was imported from Hong Kong.

The Toys (Safety) Regulations 1974 prescribe a number of safety requirements, including provisions relating to sharp points and edges. Any suspected contravention should be reported immediately to the local weights and measures authority responsible for enforcement.
Mr. Mike Thomas asked the Secretary of State for Prices and Consumer Protection whether she will take steps designed to lessen the impact of energy prices on low-income families.
Mrs. Shirley Williams: I expect to make a reference soon to the National Consumer Council on the effect of energy prices on people on low incomes.

47. Mr. David Steel asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will make a statement about his recent advice to electricity boards and social work departments in the light of the incident at Hawick where local doctors paid an overdue electricity account to preserve the health of the children of the family.

Mr. William Ross: I have no reason to believe that the liaison arrangements between the social services and the electricity boards are not operating satisfactorily in general. I have, however, arranged to obtain details of the Hawick case from the authorities concerned and will study its implications.

Mr. Gordon Wilson asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will issue a further general direction to the Scottish electricity boards to the effect that private individuals should be accepted as guarantors for the purpose of securing an electricity supply to consumers previously disconnected for non-payment of accounts.

Mr. William Ross: No general direction has been issued concerning guarantees. The acceptance of guarantors is a matter for the commercial discretion of the boards, but I am informed by the boards that they will accept private guarantors provided they are satisfied in the normal way as to their bona fides and substance.
Mr. Gordon Wilson asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what is the total sum in consumers' unclaimed deposits currently lying with (a) the SSEB and (b) the NSHEB.
Mr. William Ross: I am asking the chairmen of the boards to write to the hon. Member.

Mr. Welsh asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will give figures to show the number and monetary value of university student grants which are due but still unpaid; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. William Ross: 51,000 grants, including about 28,000 university student grants, have been paid. About 400 university students, mainly those who were late in applying, have still to be paid. Not all of these grants have been assessed and it is not possible to put a monetary value on them. The outstanding cases are being cleared as quickly as possible.
Mr. Donald Stewart asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what is the total mileage of motorways in Scotland under construction; and what is the present mileage in use.
Mr. William Ross: 15 miles of motorway are under construction in Scotland. 111 miles are at present in use.

Mr. Donald Stewart asked the Secretary of State for Scotland how many housing improvement grants were approved in the Western Isles for the last year available; and what percentage this is of the Scottish figure.

Mr. William Ross: For the period before the reorganisation of local government separate figures are not available for those areas of the former counties of Ross and Cromarty and Inverness now within the Western Isles Islands Area.

Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will detail in percentage terms the total of price rises in every one of the nationalised industries with which his Department was concerned during the past 12 months.
Mr. William Ross: The nationalised industries for which I am responsible

Mr. Donald Stewart asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what is the current strength of the fisheries protection fleet in Scotland; and how many of the vessels were at sea in each of the last six months.

Mr. William Ross: My Department's fishery protection fleet comprises six vessels. Of these one is on temporary loan to the Royal Navy and five are under my control. In each of the six months ended 31st October 1975 all five vessels were at sea.

Mr. Donald Stewart asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what representations he has had concerning the failure of the salmon fishery on the west coast in the current year; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. William Ross: Several representations have been received claiming that alleged high seas fishing for salmon this summer by foreign vessels off Lewis and Cape Wrath had a detrimental effect on salmon stocks returning to rivers in those parts. The allegations regarding foreign vessels were investigated. No evidence at all was found to suggest that these vessels, which were legitimately engaged in the mackerel fishery, were fishing for salmon.

Mr. Fairgrieve asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what extra financial help has been given to the Grampian Region and its ratepayers to offset the extra burdens they are having to bear in support of the infrastructure expenditure required to meet the requirements of the incoming and expanding oil industry.
Mr. William Ross: £2·5 million was included in the Rate Support Grant (Scotland)
raised prices in the last 12 months by the following average percentages:

I propose to continue the scheme of special assistance for oil-related expenditure in 1976–77, and local authorities' estimates of expenditure in that year are now under consideration.
Mr. Fairbairn asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what progress he has made in studying the Scottish Office's estimates with a view to making economies.

Mr. William Ross: The estimates made by the Scottish Office represent the most economic way of carrying out Government policies, though, of course, I am always alive to any opportunity of achieving further economies.

Mr. Fairbairn asked the Secretary of State for Scotland whether he will transfer an official from his present duties in the Scottish Office with a view to seeking out possible areas where economies can be made in the Scottish Office's spending, and for the formulation of plans for implementing economies and reducing staff.

Mr. William Ross: I am already arranging for the strengthening of the staff inspection teams in my Departments whose duty is to assist management to secure the economical use of staff. Part of their work is to identify areas where
603 staff reductions are possible. In addition all my staff have standing instructions to be vigilant in their search for economy in administration having regard to the duties placed on them by Parliament and public expectations of service.
Mr. Gordon Wilson asked the Secretary of State for Scotland when he expects to announce his decision on the proposed construction of an oil refinery at Nigg.
Mr. William Ross: I understand that the reporter will circulate part one of his report to parties for comment within the next few days. When he has received and taken account of comments he will
Mr. Donald Stewart asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will now raise the levels of grant and loan for crofter housing.
Mr. William Ross: I hope to make an announcement on this matter shortly.

Mr. Eldon Griffiths asked the Secretary of State for Scotland in how many cases of homicide recorded by the Scottish police the motive is considered to have been political, during the years 1972, 1973 and 1974, respectively.
Mr. William Ross: In no case of homicide in Scotland during the years 1972, 1973 and 1974 has there been any reason to suspect that political motives may have been involved.
Mr. Beith asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what forms of Exchequer aid are available for harbour improvement works in Scotland.
Mr. William Ross: The following forms of Exchequer aid are available:

Mr. Grist asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will list for each of the last three years the number of civil servants in his Department who have been prematurely retired on grounds of (i) inefficiency, (ii) limited efficiency, (iii) redundancy, and (iv) discipline, showing executive and administrative grades separately.
Mr. William Ross: The following information relates to Scottish Office staff in the Administration Group in the grades of executive officer and above:
Grants and loans under the Fisheries Act 1955 for the construction, improvement or repair of fishery marine works in order to promote the maintenance or development of the fishing industry;
Grants and loans under the Local Employment Act 1972 for the improvement of basic transport services;
Assistance to local authorities under the Countryside (Scotland) Act 1967 for improvements to make a harbour suitable for open air or water recreation by the general public; and

In exceptional circumstances, the Highlands and Islands Development Board may give financial assistance for harbour improvements, but such assistance will not in general be available concurrently with financial assistance from other Government sources.

In addition, my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for the Environment has powers under Section 11 of the Harbours Act 1964 to make loans to statutory harbour authorities for commercial harbour developments.
Mr. Trotter asked the Secretary of State for Trade to what extent fishing vessel owners will be required to pay in advance the survey fees under the Safety Provision Rules 1975.

Mr. Clinton Davis: Applicants for surveys under the Fishing Vessels (Safety Provisions) Rules 1975 are asked to deposit the whole amount of the appropriate fee at time of application, but on occasions part of the fee has been accepted with a written undertaking that the balance will be paid on completion of the survey and prior to the issue of a United Kingdom Fishing Vessel Certificate.

Mr. Trotter asked the Secretary of State for Trade whether he is satisfied that there are sufficient slipways in suitable locations around the coast to undertake the additional work necessary as a result of the Fishing Vessels Safety Provisions Rules 1975; and whether he proposes to take any steps with a view to increasing the number of slipways.

Mr. Clinton Davis: There is a shortage of slips in some areas although not in the North-East of England. There is, however, often access to suitable hards where local fishing vessels can be surveyed out of the water. For the purpose of the Fishing Vessels (Safety Provisions) Rules 1975 arrangements are being made for vessels to be seen by the Department's surveyors at the same time and place that the owner would normally take his vessel out of the water for regular maintenance or other reasons. Slipping facilities are provided on a commercial basis, and the provisions of additional facilities in a particular area would be a matter of commercial judgment.

Mr. Trotter asked the Secretary of State for Trade how many surveyors will be appointed to examine fishing vessels under the Safety Provisions Rules 1975; where they will be stationed; which areas will be covered from each position; whether a separate account will be kept for the resulting income and expenditure; what is the estimated annual income; and whether it is intended that no profit will be made on the work.

Mr. Clinton Davis: Initially 16 surveyors stationed at Aberdeen, Buckie, Fraserburgh, Leith, Grennock, Newcastle, Hull, Grimsby, Great Yarmouth, Fleet-wood, Brixham and Southampton. The five offices in Scotland cover the fleet north of the border; Hull and Newcastle cover the North-East of England south to 606 the River Humber; Grimsby covers the East of England south to the Wash, up to and including Forsdyke; Great Yarmouth covers the South-East of England from the Wash round to Bognor Regis; Southampton and Brixham cover the coast from Bognor Regis to Aberystwyth; while Fleetwood covers the remainder of Wales, the North-West of England and Northern Ireland.

Records are being kept from which it will be possible to check income from fishing vessel survey fees against the actual cost of providing the service. It was estimated that during the phasing-in period of the rules the annual revenue from fees would be as follows:
It is not intended to make either a profit or a loss on the work.

Mr. Trotter asked the Secretary of State for Trade what the requirement will be for the fitting of radios in inshore fishing vessels under the Safety Provisions Rules 1975; if these rules require vessels to carry survival suits for crew members: and, if so, what pattern or standard.

Mr. Clinton Davis: The Fishing Vessels (Safety Provisions) Rules 1975 require the carriage of portable radio equipment on fishing vessels of 17 metres in length and over. They do not require the carriage of survival suits for crew members, but work is being undertaken in consultation with manufacturers on producing a suitable specification for these.

The Merchant Shipping (Radio) (Fishing Vessels) Rules 1974 require the fitting of a medium frequency radio telephone receiver and transmitter, a loudspeaker watchkeeping receiver and two-tone signal generating equipment on fishing vessels of 12 metres in length and over operating within a prescribed area. Subject to the approval of the Secretary of State, however, very high frequency equipment may be substituted in certain circumstances where it is clear that fishing will take place within vhf range and no loss in safety will be involved.

Mr. Frank R. White asked the Secretary of State for Trade if he will make a statement on the progress of recent discussions between Her Majesty's Government and the EFTA Scandinavian countries on the subject of paper and board import quotas into the United Kingdom during 1976.

Mr. Deakins: Discussion with the main EFTA supplier countries about the levels of duty free quotas for paper and board for 1976 are now nearing completion. The full representations made by the industry about its difficulties are being carefully taken into account throughout these discussions. There will be very few increases in the quota levels for 1976; these will include some minor adjustments and small increases in products which are not produced in the United Kingdom in sufficient quantities. I do not think a further statement is necessary as my right hon. Friend expects shortly to be able to lay an order before the House covering these quota levels.
Mr. Frank R. White asked the Secretary of State for Trade what were the total imports of paper and board from the EFTA Scandinavian countries to the United Kingdom over the past five years,

tr.td: Estimates for the whole of 1975 are not available.
* Implied consumption is production plus imports minus exports, adjusted for known stock changes.

Mr. Deakins: The question of reimposing duties on knitted outerwear of Tariff Heading No. 6005 is under urgent consideration but presents a number 608 expressed in tons and as a percentage of home consumption, giving best estimates for 1975.

Mr. Deakins: Production, imports and implied consumption of paper and board in the United Kingdom in the past five years and in the first half of 1975 were as follows:

Before duties can be reimposed under the procedures of Protocol 1 of the Portuguese/EEC Free Trade Agreement a regulation by the EEC Commission and an order under the Import Duties Act must be made.

section.title: London and Counties Securities Group Ltd.

body.p:
Mr. Ted Fletcher asked the Secretary of State for Trade on what date he
609 received his inspector's report into the business activities of London and Counties Securities Group Ltd.
Mr. Clinton Davis: 7th March 1975.

Sir G. de Freitas asked the Secretary of State for Trade what action he proposes to take to prevent Spanish steel being dumped in the United Kingdom at prices more than 25 per cent. lower than those prevailing in Spain for the same Spanish steel.

Mr. Deakins: My Department announced on Thursday, 6th November that it had accepted for investigation an application for the imposition of antidumping duties under the Customs Duties (Dumping and Subsidies) Act 1969 on imports of plain or deformed steel reinforcing bars or rods originating in Spain. The outcome of this investigation will determine what action will be taken. No allegations of dumping of other types of steel from Spain have been made to my Department.

Dr. Glyn asked the Secretary of State for Trade if he will reconsider his decision regarding grants for double glazing in the Windsor and Maidenhead areas, in view of the recent increase in aircraft noise under and adjacent to flight paths.

Mr. Clinton Davis: An extensively improved Noise Insulation Grant Scheme for Heathrow came into force on 1st July 1975. The outer area was determined by reference to the 55 Noise and Number Index contour and comprises, with minor exceptions, all wards and parishes of which any part is within the 55 NNI contour for 1974 traffic. It is unlikely that any changes in traffic patterns have been sufficient to bring new areas within that contour.
Lord James Douglas-Hamilton asked the Secretary of State for Trade (1) if he will take steps to ensure that a noise insulation grants scheme map will be accurate before it is applied;

(3) how many residents within the constituency of Edinburgh, West, if any, would qualify for a grant under the terms of the Draft Noise Insulation Grant Scheme Map, put forward by the BAA for application at Turnhouse Airport;

(4) whether he will ensure that the Noise Insulation Grants Scheme Map, drawn up by the BAA for application at Turnhouse, will be revised when the precise noise levels have been fully established once the new runway becomes operational, so that the Noise Insulation Grant Scheme Map can be confirmed as being accurate;
(5) if he will ensure that when the new runway at Turnhouse Airport becomes operational, the precise noise levels will be established through monitoring;

(6) if he will ensure that the Draft Noise Insulation Grants Scheme Map, drawn up by the BAA for application at Turnhouse will be carefully compared by the Department of Trade, with the Noise Insulation Grants Scheme Map which apply to Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Manchester;

(7) if he will ensure that the Noise Insulation Grants Scheme to be eventually introduced by the BAA in the vicinity of Turnhouse Airport, will not be inferior in any respect to the Noise Insulation Grants Schemes introduced at Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Manchester, and that residents living near Turnhouse will experience no more noise at night than those living near Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Manchester Airports;
(8) whether residents residing in Ministry of Defence properties in the vicinity of Craighall will qualify for a grant under any Noise Insulation Grant Scheme introduced by the BAA.

Mr. Clinton Davis: On 21st July, in answer to a Question from my hon. Friend the Member for Edinburgh, Central (Mr. Cook), I told the House—[Vol. 896, c. 25]—that the British Airports Authority, which is the owner and manager of Edinburgh Airport, was able and willing to bring into operation appropriate noise abatement measures, including
611 the provision of a noise insulation grant scheme, and that I, therefore, did not deem it necessary to designate the airport and assume direct responsibility for these matters. I understand that the BAA has since then had detailed discussions with the Airport Consultative Committee and local interests about them. I have drawn the hon. Member's Questions to the attention of the chairman of the authority and have suggested that he should get into touch with the hon. Member and offer to discuss matters of detail relating to noise abatement and noise insulation in the vicinity of Edinburgh Airport, such as those raised in these Questions.

Mr. Cant asked the Secretary of State for Trade whether he will appoint inspectors to investigate the position of the Lifeguard Assurance Company under Section 165 of the Companies Act 1967, following its decision not to accept new business, as a consequence of its undercapitalisation in relation to the volume of business it has written.
Mr. Clinton Davis: No.

Mr. Michael Morris asked the Secretary of State for Trade how many staff were employed by his Department in February 1974 and in October 1974; how many are employed at the present time; and what increase, if any, he expects for 1975 and 1976.

Mr. Deakins: On 1st April 1974, the first date for which information was collected following the creation of my Department, there were 7,071 staff in post, the corresponding numbers on 1st October 1974 and 1st October 1975 being 7,209 and 7,689 respectively. By 1st April 1976 staff in post are expected to total 7,766 with little change throughout the rest of the year.

Mr. Michael Morris asked the Secretary of State for Trade for what reasons any extra staff were recruited by his Department between February 1974 and the present; and for what reasons any extra staff will be recruited in the rest of 1975.

Mr. Deakins: Extra staff have been recruited since March 1974, when my Department was created, mainly in order 612 to meet a temporary increase of work on the impending transfer of the Companies Registration Office to Cardiff; to undertake extra work in the Insolvency Service and on the surveillance monitoring of imports of textiles; to provide enhanced services to exporters; and to fill hitherto existing vacancies throughout the department. Any recruitment of extra staff during the rest of 1975 is likely to arise from the work of the Insolvency Service and the Companies Registration Office.
Mr. Michael Morris asked the Secretary of State for Trade what is the number of unfilled vacancies in his Department, for which recruits are required but have not yet been found.
Mr Deakins: Recruits are currently required for 29 of the vacancies in the approved staffing establishment for my Department to 1st April next.

Mr. Madden asked the Secretary of State for Trade how many inquiries are being conducted by his Department into the affairs of private companies; how many such inquiries have been initiated in the past three years; and on what dates inquiry reports were published in the same period.

Mr. Clinton Davis: I assume my hon. Friend is referring to investigations under the Companies Act 1948. Inquiries into the affairs of 30 private companies have not yet been completed. Since 1st November 1972 inspectors have been appointed in 33 private companies, 13 of which are connected with inquiries into public companies. It has been the practice of successive Governments not to publish inspectors' reports on private companies unless there is a public interest or the inquiry is connected with another inquiry into a public company.

In addition, since 1st November 1972 inquiries under Section 109 of the Companies Act 1967 have been instituted in respect of some 350 private companies. I am not empowered to publish the information so obtained.
