Mr. Jim Lester asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what relative importance he attaches in planning terms to the Nottinghamshire-Derby Sub-regional Study, the proposed structure plan, and the interim statement of planning policy issued by the Nottinghamshire County Council on 30th July.

Mr. Oakes: The Nottinghamshire-Derbyshire Sub-regional study, published in 1969, was commissioned by the county councils of Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire, the then County Borough Council of Derby, and the City Council of Nottingham. Pending the preparation of structure plans it has formed the basis for considering the needs, potential for development, and major land uses in the two county areas. It has no statutory force.

The structure plan for Nottinghamshire will be the major planning document for the county area. It will establish the broad structural policies for land use and transportation, and will provide the basis for the detailed land allocations and development control policies to be worked out in local plans.

An interim statement of planning policy—issued by a County Council under Paragraph 32(d) (IV) of Schedule 16 to the Local Government Act 1972—is not subject to the approval of the Secretary of State. Its purpose is to set out certain considerations which the district councils in the county must take into account in deciding whether a planning application which comes before them is a "county matter". It does not in itself constitute a planning decision; any specific application to carry out development must be decided under the normal planning procedures.
Mr. Jim Lester asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what is the up-to-date estimate of his Department's contribution towards the Nottinghamshire structure plan and its likely total cost.

Mr. Oakes: The responsibility for preparing the Nottinghamshire structure plan lies with the council of that county. Following the usual practice, the Department will be advising the county council on the technical and procedural aspects of structure plan preparation and on the implications of Government policies for the structure plan area.

The total cost of preparing the plan is a matter for the county council, which would doubtless be able to help the hon. Member in that connection. The cost of the Department's contribution cannot readily be assessed but will not be substantial.

Mr. Macfarlane asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will list the various sport and recreation reports and inquiries initiated by the Minister for Sport and called for since March 1974; and if he will indicate the progress of each one.
Mr. Denis Howell: The White Paper on Sport and Recretation published last August (Cmnd 6200) outlined the major proposals I have initiated.

Since the White Paper was published I have announced proposals for the formation of a sports aid foundation to raise funds to assist our sportsmen and sportswomen in their preparation and training for international competition. At the same time, my working party on centres of excellence is carrying out a thorough investigation of the provision of practical assistance at educational establishments.

Since the beginning of the current football season the Football Grounds Improvement Trust has been raising funds for disbursement at the trustees' discretion to assist clubs to meet the cost of improvements to football grounds. The problem of football hooliganism is under continuous review by my working party, which has issued detailed recommendations to clubs for both domestic and European matches and has developed with the organisations concerned a number of improvements in arrangements for rail and coach transport.

Mr. Fairbairn asked the Secretary of State for the Environment, with reference to answer to Written Question on 4th November 1975, which explains that 120 limes were purchased for New Palace Yard at a cost of £600 from the Rosalinda Rose Gardens and that 82 have been planted and 38 held in reserve, why his Department ordered 38 more trees than were needed; and what is to happen to the trees held in reserve now that it has been decided to uproot the original 82.

Mr. Armstrong: In any major landscaping work, more stock is ordered than will actually be planted, to ensure adequate reserves in case of failure. The surplus stock is grown on in the Department's nursery, and is used elsewhere if not needed to provide replacements.

Sir John Gilmour asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what saving, if any, will accrue from the centralisation of vehicles and driving licences at Swansea once all the issues by local offices have terminated.

Dr. Gilbert: No detailed comparison of cost between the local authority driver and vehicle licensing system and the centralised arrangements has been undertaken, because licensing would not have remained viable under the local system. Such indicators as there are, however, suggest that continuance of a local system would have required more staff than the centralised system, and that any additional costs incurred on the centralised system—in terms of buildings and equipment—will be at least offset by the benefits which can be expected from centralisation, such as reduced evasion of vehicle excise duty and tighter control over driving offenders.

Mr. Ronald Atkins asked the Secretary of State for the Environment whether any independent management studies, other than the Research Report by Gareth Morgan, have been made of the Central Lancashire Development Corporation; and whether they were favourable or unfavourable.
Mr. Oakes: I am not aware of any.

Mr. Oakes: I have no knowledge of the number of times these committees were consulted by the Central Lancashire Development Corporation, but I understand that representatives of the Corporation took part in many of the 30 meetings which have taken place over the past two years.

Member for Preston, North on 4th November 1975.
Mr. Oakes: Yes—even though the report did not raise issues which needed reference to my Department.

(7) what has been the turnover of Central Lancashire Development Corporation staff employed within physical planning, social facilities and research and comprising inclusively grades 6 to the upper salary range.

Central Lancashire Development Corporation is no exception. Inquiries of this nature should therefore be made to them direct.

Mr. Ronald Atkins asked the Secretary of State for the Environment (1) if he will request the Central Lancashire Development Corporation to implement the objectives expressed on page 8 of the Research Report by Gareth Morgan;

Mr. Oakes: Decisions on whether or not this research report should be published, or its objectives implemented, are entirely matters for the development corporation to decide.

Mr. Cordle asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if, in order to assist in the democratic control of planning, he will introduce appropriate legislation to prevent any administrative county council 702 from proceeding with any major road project unless that project has been approved and sanctioned by the district councils of the area directly involved.

Dr. Gilbert: No. Parliament in the Local Government Act 1972 has allocated different functions to the various levels of local government. District councils already have the right to enter formal objections to road proposals.

Mr. Alan Lee Williams asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will list all the road schemes in London; how many properties have been bought for each one; and what are the projected starting dates for all these road schemes.

Dr. Gilbert: I regret that the full information asked for by the hon. Member could be brought together only at disproportionate cost, but a list of road proposals, involving more than £250,000 each, in Greater London, as at 31st March 1975, will be found in "Roads in England" 1974–75, Tables 5, 6 and 7.

Mr. Cordle asked the Secretary of State for the Environment how many incidents of oil pollution affecting coastal waters have been reported to his Department in the past 12 months; and what has been the cost to the Exchequer of undertaking necessary remedial measures.

Mr. Denis Howell: The maintenance of comprehensive records of incidents of oil on or near the shore was introduced in July 1975. Since then, local authorities in England have reported 42 incidents. Such costs as arise have been met by the local authorities concerned, and there has been no direct cost to the Exchequer.
My right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for Trade maintains records of oil sighted at sea.

Mr. Michael Latham asked the Secretary of State for the Environment whether the Minister for Housing and Construction has met a deputation of the National Council of Building Material Producers since 3rd July; and what was the outcome of the meeting.
Mr. Freeson: I met representatives of the National Council of Building Material Producers on 7th August. We had a useful discussion about the problems facing the industry.

Mr. Michael Latham asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what progress has been made since 7th July by his departmental inquiry into the use of woodwool formwork for concrete floors; and whether he will make a statement.

Mr. Freeson: The Fire Research Station is carrying out tests to evaluate the fire resistance in structures where woodwool slabs have been used, but these are not likely to be completed for six months. In the meantime, a number of buildings in which this material has been used have been examined, but have revealed no evidence that there is any immediate risk to safety.

Mr. Michael Latham asked the Secretary of State for the Environment how many times the external members of his Review of Housing Finance have so far met; and when he expects that the work will be completed and the review published.

Mr. Freeson: My right hon. Friend's advisory group has so far met five times. I expect that the work of the review of housing finance will be completed and its conclusions published in the spring or early summer of next year.

Mr. Michael Latham asked the Secretary of State for the Environment whether he is now in a position to name the members of the Construction Exports Advisory Board, the setting up of which he first announced on 7th August.
Mr. Freeson: Not yet, but I shall make an announcement soon.

Mr. Michael Latham asked the Secretary of State for the Environment on what dates his Department received, in completed form (a) Mr. George Dobry's interim report on the Development Con- 704 trol System, (b) his report entitled "Control of Demolition" and (c) his final report on the Development Control System; and when he expects to be in a position to make a statement on his policy regarding the recommendations of these three reports.

Mr. John Silkin: In January 1974, September 1974 and February 1975, respectively, As to a statement, I would refer the hon. Member to my reply today to my hon. Friend the Member for Walsall, South (Mr. George).

Mr. George asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what conclusions he has reached on the recommendations made by Mr. George Dobry QC in his Final Report of the Review of the Development Control System and in his report on Control of Demolition; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. John Silkin: My right hon. Friends and I have now completed our consideration of Mr. Dobry's reports. In doing so we have had the benefit of comments from all the local authority associations, who participated in a working party which examined each recommendation in detail. We also received the views of developers and of some 50 other organisations who have an interest in development control, and we are most grateful for their helpful observations.

I should like once again to express our thanks to Mr. Dobry, to his advisory group, and to all those who contributed to the preparation of his reports. The review has provided a unique insight into the detailed working of the system, and contains many valuable proposals for improving its administration.

Mr. Dobry made more than 100 recommendations, and many of those consulted put forward views on most or all of them. On many, there was almost complete unanimity of view, and a welcome was extended to Mr. Dobry's proposals. In particular, few dissented from Mr. Dobry's general conclusion that the existing development control system is fundamentally sound, but on two of his major recommendations—(1), the division of applications into two categories subject to different statutory procedures and (2), the further control of demolition—there has been a divergence of view. In both cases it seems to us that the weight of argument—and for
705 that matter of numbers also—is in favour of rejection and we do not propose to accept either of these recommendations.

In the interests of brevity I give our reasons in full in a statement which I have placed in the Library. I also place on record there our conclusions on all the other recommendations and the steps we propose to take with regard to them. It is my intention to issue a circular to local authorities in the near future on administrative matters. Where administrative action is required of the Department of the Environment and the Welsh Office, it has already been put in hand. Other matters needing fresh legislation must await a convenient opportunity, which I hope may be not long delayed.

Mr. Michael Latham asked the Secretary of State for the Environment whether he will set out in tabular form the number of dwellings in Great Britain at the end of December 1974 which were owner-occupied, rented from public authorities, privately rented and subject to other forms of tenure, respectively, giving also the total dwelling stock and the percentage represented by each tenure.

Mr. Armstrong: Estimates based on results of the 1971 Census, which did not distinguish between privately rented housing and "other" forms of tenure, appear on page 73 of Housing and Construction Statistics No. 13, a copy of which is available in the Library. "Other" tenures probably account for about 5 per cent. of the total stock and comprise dwellings, in public or private ownership, that are rented with farms or business premises or are occupied by virtue of employment.

Mr. Michael Latham asked the Secretarary of State for the Environment what representations he has received from the Royal Institute of British Architects about his proposals for more extensive use of the design-and-construction method of building; and what reply he has sent.

Mr. Freeson: I am considering a memorandum received on 3rd November from the Royal Institute of British Architects on design services for housing, which makes references to design and build procedures.

Mr. Michael Latham asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what progress is being made in his consideration of the Wood Report entitled "The Public Client and the Construction Industries"; and when he expects to be in a position to give more detailed guidance to public sector clients on the recommendations of the report.

Mr. Freeson: My Department will take account of the report in producing a code of procedures on housebuilding, to consolidate and bring up to date its advice to local authorities. As this will take some time to complete, sections of the code will be issued as they are ready. The guidance in respect of public sector work other than housing is being considered by Departments concerned.

Mr. Michael Latham asked the Secretary of State for the Environment whether Her Majesty's Government have yet implemented the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora; and whether he will make a statement on his policy on this matter.
Mr. Denis Howell: The Government intend to implement the convention on 1st January 1976. The final details are being settled and an announcement will be made shortly.
Mr. Michael Latham asked the Secretary of State for the Environment when he expects to bring into operation that section of the Control of Pollution Act 1974 dealing with noise abatement.
Mr. Denis Howell: I expect that, subject to parliamentary approval, Part III of the Control of Pollution Act 1974 will commence in England and Wales from 1st January 1976.
Mr. Body asked the Secretary of State for the Environment (1) what is the estimated cost of his Department's proposal to build the Holbeach Bypass, the A17 road from Saracens Head to Laurel Lodge;

(2) whether his Department has calculated the probable cost of constructing the Holbeach bypass, the A17 road from Saracens Head to Laurel Lodge, according to the proposals of the Holbeach Parish Council.
Mr. Carmichael: The current estimated cost of constructing a new road between Saracen's Head and Laurel Lodge is £2,150,000. No alternative proposal has yet been submitted by Holbeach Parish Council.

Sir G. de Freitas asked the Secretary of State for the Environment approximately how many road fund licences were issued to people having addresses in the Kettering and Corby areas, respectively, in 1974, 1972, 1970 and 1968.
Mr. Carmichael: Records have not been kept in such a way as to allow this information to be made available.
Sir G. de Freitas asked the Secretary of State for the Environment which local authorities in the East Midlands have responsibility for homelessness.

Mr. Armstrong: All social services authorities have a duty under Section 21(1) (b) of the National Assistance Act 1948 to provide temporary accommodation in certain circumstances for persons in urgent need. The joint circular on Homelessness—DOE 18/74—recommended that housing authorities should increasingly accept prime responsibility for the homeless. The information I have is that in the East Midlands all but three housing authorities have accepted some measure of responsibility.
Mr. Geoffrey Finsberg asked the Secretary of State for Environment if he will now make a statement on the content of lead in petrol.

Mr. Denis Howell: The Government is considering what change of policy regarding lead in petrol is needed in the light of the review announced last December by my right hon. Friend the then Secretary of State for Energy which is now nearing completion. It is necessary at the same time to take account 708 of current proposals in the European Community for legislation to control airborne lead.
It is hoped to provide an opportunity for the House to debate these proposals and to make a full statement at that time.

Mr. Peter Morrison asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what was the average rate increase for district councils as opposed to county councils in 1974–75; and what percentage of the district councils increased their rates by (i) more than 40 per cent., (ii) less than 40 per cent. but more than 30 per cent., (iii) less than 30 per cent. but more than 20 per cent., (iv) less than 20 per cent. but more than 10 per cent. and (v) less than 10 per cent., respectively.
Mr. Oakes: I understand that the hon. Member is seeking a comparison between the rates levied in 1975–76 and 1974–75.

The increase in the average precept levied by county councils is not yet available; I shall write to the hon. Member when this is known. The increase in the average non-domestic rate poundage for district councils—which includes the county precept—in 1975–76 is 23 per cent. This figures excludes London.

Mr. George Cunningham asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he has ruled out the possibility of a London rate equalisation scheme for 1976–77 which does not provide for all the inner boroughs to pay in and all the outer boroughs to draw out.

Mr. Oakes: No possibilities have been ruled out, but the present proposals under discussion with the London Boroughs Association involve some equalisation payment between the inner and outer boroughs.

Mr. Evelyn King asked the Secretary of State for the Environment how much in salaries was paid to local government officials immediately prior to reorganisation, two months after reorganisation and at the last convenient date, respectively; and what numbers were employed on the same dates.

Mr. Oakes: This information is not available but total expenditure on salaries and wages by local authorities in England and Wales in the financial years 1973–74 and 1974–75 was £4,386 million and £5,747 million (provisional), respectively. As regards the number of local government employees in England and Wales I would refer the hon. Member to the Answer I gave on 17th October to the hon. Member for Ashford (Mr. Speed)—[Vol. 897, c. 826]

Mr. George Cunningham asked the Secretary of State for the Environment (1) how many communications have been received from the Law Society about the regulations on the control of notices to quit to be made under Secton 123 of the Housing Act 1974; and when the latest communication was received;
(2) whether he has consulted any person or body outside Government about the implementation of Section 123 of the Housing Act 1974 besides the Law Society;
(3) on what date the Law Society was first consulted about regulations on the control of notices to quit to be made under Section 123 of the Housing Act 1974.

Mr. Freeson: The Law Society was asked on 16th June for advice on the form of the information to be contained in notices to quit. One communication only has been received from them, and this was sent on 9th July. No other body or person outside Government has been asked for advice or consulted.
Mr. Dalyell asked the Secretary of State for the Environment when he expects to announce his overall transport policy; and what form the announcement will take.
Mr. Crosland: I refer my hon. Friend to the reply I gave on 5th November to the hon. Member for Shipley (Mr. Fox)—[Vol. 889, c. 206.]

Mr. Spearing asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what criteria are applied by his inspectors in determining whether houses are fit or unfit in respect of orders made under Part III of the Housing Act 1957.
Mr. Armstrong: The statute lays down various criteria, including such matters as repair and stability, freedom from damp, drainage and sanitary conveniences, etc.

Mr. Spearing asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what criteria are used by his inspectors in determining whether houses, designated by them as unfit in respect of Part III of the Housing Act 1957, can best be dealt with by rehabilitation or by clearance.

Mr. Armstrong This is a matter for the professional judgment of the inspector, who will necessarily have regard to the statutory provisions and to the guidance given from time to time in departmental circulars.
Further advice on the social and economic aspects of both redevelopment and rehabilitation issues is being prepared.

Mr. Stanbrook asked the Secretary of State for the Environment how many administrators, including clerical and publicity workers, there were in British Rail in the years 1971, 1972, 1973 and 1974, respectively.

Mr. Carmichael: British Rail has provided the following figures:
1971 29,003
1972 28,436
1973 27,901
1974 27,922

Mr. Spearing asked the Secretary of State for the Environment which types or categories of local authority in England and Wales can incur expenditure in public advertisements designed to inform employers or industrialists of the advantages or facilities for industry in
711 their area; and if he will extend such powers to the Docklands Joint Committee of London.

Mr. Oakes: The powers to which my hon. Friend refers are available to local authorities in England and Wales outside London. The Greater London Council has suggested that these powers should be extended to local authorities in Greater London, and we are considering this.

Mr. Spearing asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what progress has been made in the fitting of sound insulation to dwellings along Newham Way (A13); and if he is satisfied with the speed of implementation of the agreed scheme.
Mr. Carmichael: 244 offers of insulation have been made and the first tenders were invited on 6th November, with further tender invitations going out at fortnightly intervals.
Work on the high-rise flats will start early in 1976, and it is confidently expected that the scheme will be completed in that year.
In view of the difficult nature of the work on this particular scheme, I am satisfied with the progress being made.
Mr. Michael Marshall asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what was the amount spent by his Department on advertising in national daily and Sunday newspapers in each month of 1975.

Mr. O'Halloran asked the Secretary of State for the Environment when he expects to let local authorities have the necessary forms as prescribed under Section 89 of the Housing Act 1974; and if he will give an explanation for the delay.
Mr. Armstrong: I shall write to my hon. Friend.
Mr. O'Halloran asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what plans he has for any further road widening of the Al-Ml link from Inner London to Hendon; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Carmichael: At this stage I have nothing to add to my right hon. Friend's statement of 21st October 1975 on the Greater London Development Plan.

Mr. Ridley asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will estimate the yield of the rents of all public sector housing in 1954–55 and in 1974–75, respectively; and if he will also give the approximate market value of those rents in a free market for each year.
Mr. Armstrong: I shall write to the hon. Member.
Mr. Freud asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will list the countries from which hauliers granted European Economic Community permits operate.
Mr. Carmichael: All nine member States of the European Economic Community.
Mr. Freud asked the Secretary of State for the Environment how many European Economic Community permits for road hauliers were issued in 1975.
Mr. Carmichael: 2,363, of which the United Kingdom received 272.

Mr. Freud asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what were the criteria used by the Department in assessing whether or not an application for European Economic Community permits, 1975, be granted to hauliers.
Mr. Carmichael: Evidence of ability to make fullest use of the permits, normally through experience of international road haulage.

Mr. Loyden asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what was the cost of running the Merseyside County Council for the years ended 31st March 1974 and 31st March 1975; and what will be the estimated cost for the year ending 31st March 1976.
Mr. Oakes: I shall write to my hon. Friend.
Mr. Loyden asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what was the number of people employed by the Merseyside County Council at present; and what is the estimated number for 1976–77.

Mr. Oakes: This information is not available centrally. Local authorities are responsible for planning their own manpower requirements in the light of their individual circumstances and of the constraints of national policy which require an overall standstill in expenditure in 1976–77.

Mr. Frank R. White asked the Secretary of State for the Environment what regulations he has laid down concerning the manufacture or storage of explosive and volatile products within close proximity to residential areas.
Mr. Harold Walker: I have been asked to reply.

The Chairman of the Health and Safety Commission informs me that the manufacture and storage of hazardous substances in general are controlled by the Health and Safety at Work, Etc., Act 1974 and the relevant statutory provisions listed by that Act. In particular, the manufacture and storage of explosives are controlled by the Explosives Act 1875 and regulations and licensing arrangements made under that Act. Keeping of petroleum spirit and petroleum mixtures is subject to licensing by local authorities under the Petroleum (Consolidation) Act 1928.
The use and storage of certain other flammable liquids in factories are controlled by the Highly Flammable Liquids and Liquefied Petroleum Gases Regulations, 1972.

Mr. Frank R. White asked the Secretary of State for the Environment if, in view of the concern of residents of Bury and Radcliffe living near the Tetrosyl development about the dangerous nature of the operations to be carried out there, he will ascertain the position with regard to the adequacy of the safety measures at the installation; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Harold Walker: I have been asked to reply.
I have been informed by the Chairman of the Health and Safety Commission that two projects which involve liquids which are highly flammable are proceeding at the factory of Tetrosyl Ltd., Bury.

The first is a proposal to construct a number of steel tanks for the storage of highly flammable paint thinners on the site of a former mill pond situated near the gate of the factory. Such a development is subject both to planning controls and to licensing by the fire authority under the Petroleum Consolidation Act
715 1928. Before the development is allowed to proceed further the most careful attention will be paid to the safety of work people and the public.
The second project is the construction within the factory of a 12-ton butane storage installation.

Detailed advice on the safety of this installation has been given by HMFI, and the completed plant will conform with this advice. The advice is based on current codes of practice, and it takes into account the safety of work people, members of the public and adjoining buildings and installations.

Mr. Hannam asked the Secretary of State for the Environment (1) if he will list the proportion of accidents involving injury to the driver between invalid tricycles, normal three-wheelers, DHSS cars and normal four-wheeled cars, respectively, for England, during the years ended 30th September 1973, 1974 and 1975;

(2) what was the injury accident rate per million miles for invalid tricycles, adapted cars issued by the DHSS and normal cars and taxis for the 12 months to 30th September 1973, 1974 and 1975, respectively;
INJURY ACCIDENTS FOR SPECIFIED CLASSES OF VEHICLES: ENGLAND

body.p: Mr. John Garrett asked the Minister for the Civil Service how many HEOs(A) have been appointed, and what proportions were educated at public schools,

(3) if he will list the proportion of single-vehicle accidents involving injury to the driver of invalid tricycles, normal three-wheelers, DHSS cars and normal four-wheeled cars, respectively, for England, during the years ended 30th September 1973, 1974 and 1975, respectively.
Dr. Gilbert, pursuant to his reply [Official Report, 6th November 1975; Vol. 899, c. 294], circulated the following reply:
The available information comes from two sources, as shown in the tables below.

First, injury accidents, reported to the police, which involve invalid tricycles and casualties to their occupants. This detail, which forms part of the regular statistics of the Department of the Environment, is available only since 1974; no separate data is available for DHSS cars.

Second, the injury accidents to users of invalid tricycles and to DHSS cars are available from DHSS statistics for years ending 30th September. These statistics may include injury accidents not necessarily reported to the police, and relate to the years in which accidents are reported to the DHSS; police reports refer to dates when accidents occurred.
The differences in definitions and procedures account for the differing rates for invalid tricycle accidents as shown by the two sources.
were graduates of Oxford or Cambridge universities and were arts graduates.
Mr. Charles R. Morris: I regret that the information is not immediately available. I am having it collected and will write to my hon. Friend as soon as possible.

44. Mr. Sillars asked the Lord Advocate how many of his staff are engaged whole-time and part-time in the preparatory work for the possible transfer of Scottish law functions to the proposed Scottish Assembly.

The Lord Advocate: Five members of my staff have been engaged during the last year in work connected with the Government's devolution proposals, including an examination of the problems arising in the field of law functions. Although it has not been possible for any of these officials to deal whole-time with this work several of them have devoted a very large part of their time to it.

Mr. Corbett asked the Lord President of the Council whether he will consider a scheme to provide pre-paid envelopes addressed to the House of Commons, London SW1, in all post offices for issue on demand to the registered unemployed, retirement pensioners, widows, the disabled and those on supplementary benefit claimable on production of the appropriate benefit or pension book.

Mr. Edward Short: I would refer my hon. Friend to the answer which my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for Industry gave him on 29th October about concessionary postal rates—[Vol. 898, c. 542]. I do not think a special concession for correspondence with Members of this House is justified.
Mr. Onslow asked the Lord President of the Council what is the cost to public funds in the current year of first-class official paid envelopes for the use of hon. Members.
Mr. Edward Short: The cost for the year ended 31st October 1975 was £194,846, of which £181,958 is attributable to postal charges and £12,888 represents the cost of envelopes supplied.
Mr. Onslow asked the Lord President of the Council why supplies of second-class official paid envelopes are not as readily available throughout the House of Commons as first-class envelopes.

Mr. Edward Short: The Services Committee considered the position earlier in the Session in the light of existing postal charges and decided that no change should be made in the present arrangements. It can certainly be looked at again if this is the wish of most Members.

Mr. Cyril Smith asked the Lord President of the Council if he will set out in the Official Report a comparative table of the number of hours spent by Members of Parliament in Standing Committees and Select Committees in each of the last five Sessions of Parliament.

Mr. Edward Short: No records are kept of the number of hours spent by Members either in Standing Committees or in Select Committees. The numbers of times Members attend Committees are given in the Official Returns ordered at the close of each Session which are made available in the Library.

Mr. Ashley asked the Attorney-General if he will propose a ban on the legal representation of Government Departments, landlords, employers and others appearing before tribunals until a system of legal representation available to all parties before tribunals is introduced.
The Attorney-General: No.

Mr. Nicholas Winterton asked the Lord President of the Council what was the cost to his Department of placing the advertisement in the Daily Express newspaper on 8th November which quoted statements from Mr. Campbell Adamson and Mr. Len Murray.

Mr. Edward Short: No such advertisement appeared in the Daily Express
719 newspaper on 8th November. The advertisement quoting statements from Mr. Campbell Adamson and Mr. Len Murray appeared in the Daily Express on 10th November at a total cost of £6,160.

Mr. Edward Short: The numbers of pages added to the statute book since the 1970–71 Session are as follows:

Mr. Warren asked the Secretary of State for Defence how many European countries, besides the United Kingdom, taking part in the current study of the Boeing E3A, AWACS, aircraft have paid their share of the cost of the study.

Mr. William Rodgers: NATO studies of an AEW system based on the Boeing E3A AWACS aircraft are currently being funded by the United States, Canada, Germany, France and the United Kingdom. Italy has also agreed to participate in the funding. Contributions are being made on the understanding that if the project goes ahead the costs of the studies will be subsumed in the costs of the procurement programme.
Mr. Warren asked the Secretary of State for Defence why the ban on the export of Jaguar aircraft to Egypt has now been lifted.
Mr. Wiliam Rodgers: I have nothing to add to what I told the hon. Member 720 for Woking (Mr. Onslow) on 11th November.

Mr. McCusker asked the Secretary of State for Defence how many UDR men have been murdered in County Armagh since the Regiment's inception; and how many regular soldiers have been murdered in County Armagh since 1969.
Mr. John: Fourteen members of the Ulster Defence Regiment and 52 regular soldiers have been killed in County Armagh since 1969.
Mr. McCusker asked the Secretary of State for Defence if he will outline in detail the appeals procedure to the Defence Council which is open to a discharged member of the UDR.

Mr. John: Under the regulations, a discharged member of the UDR who desires to appeal to the Defence Council should forward his appeal through the appropriate channel. This would normally be to his former commanding officer in the first instance, who would forward the appeal through his headquarters to the Ministry of Defence. The decision of the Defence Council is conveyed personally to the applicant in writing. The decision of the Defence Council is final.

Mr. McCusker asked the Secretary of State for Defence how many of the 82 members of the UDR from 2 and 11 UDR Battalions who were discharged during the period 1st January 1975 and 31st October 1975 without tendering their resignations were told the reasons for their discharge.

Mr. John: The regulations provide a number of specific causes of discharge. All were informed of the cause in accordance with these regulations. It is not possible to give details of any further information which may have been given by the commanding officer in any particular case.

Mr. David Young asked the Secretary of State for Defence whether any redundancies are contemplated at Hawker Siddeley Dynamics factory at Lostock in the period 1975 to 1980 as a result of the cancellation of the Sub-Martel project.

Mr. William Rodgers: Cancellation of Sub-Martel will have no immediate effect
721 on Lostock and it is expected that the factory will have an expanding guided weapons workload from 1976–77 for the rest of the decade as work on XJ521—the United Kingdom development of a homing head and fuse for the United States Sparrow missile—builds up. Given a reasonable continuation of Hawker Siddeley Dynamics' commercial orders there should therefore be no redundancies in that timescale.

Mr. David Young asked the Secretary of State for Defence what efforts his Department is making to replace the shortfall which will result from the development work lost by the cancellation of the Sub-Martel project.

Mr. William Rodgers: I have held detailed discussions with both the management and trade unions at Hawker Siddeley Dynamics to consider the immediate employment implications of the cancellation of Sub-Martel. As regards the longer term, there are a number of possible future missile requirements which are now being examined but no decisions on these can be taken at the present time.

In order to preserve the company's capability to meet these future requirements, it has already been announced that the company's current air-to-air test vehicle programme is being extended and that Hawker Siddeley Dynamics will act as the British systems contractor for NATO feasibility studies on a second generation anti-ship missile. A contract has also been let for the use of the Sub-Martel discharge test vehicle for use in the general context of submarine torpedo discharge systems. In addition there are a number of items of research which are being discussed with the company.
Mr. Geoffrey Finsberg asked the Secretary of State for Defence if he will make a statement about the reconstruction of the Dockyards Board and the Dockyards Trading Fund.

Mr. William Rodgers: As part of our continuing search for improved efficiency in the Royal Dockyards, we recently reviewed the management structure with a view to deciding when and how progress might best be made in the further implementation of the Mallabar Report. 722 As a result, reorganisation of the Dockyards Policy Board has taken place with a view to increasing the authority of the Chief Executive Dockyards, who is now the Board's deputy Chairman. Other changes that have taken place involve a new Dockyard wage structure on trial at Chatham and a related plan for improving the control of Dockyard work. A separate Dockyard Vote will come into operation on 1st April next year.

The need now, therefore, is for a period of stability in order that these changes can be fully implemented and the resulting experience assessed. During this time we shall concentrate on implementing planned improvements in management, production programming, manpower planning, financial control and cost accounting. We shall also pursue an up-to-date approach to industrial relations and wages policy. We intend to take a firm decision on the introduction of a Dockyards Trading Fund by January 1978.

Mr. Michael Latham asked the Prime Minister whether, pursuant to his reply to the hon. Member for Melton on 15th July, he is now in a position to transfer licensing responsibility for the importation of live crocodiles and other exotic wild creatures from the Department of Trade to the Department of the Environment.

The Prime Minister: We intend to implement the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora on 1st January 1976, and this licensing responsibility will be transferred to the Department of the Environment at the same time.

Mr. John Smith: We intend to take all appropriate steps to encourage the placing of orders for production platforms with United Kingdom yards, including the two which are being established with Government assistance.

Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of State for Energy whether it is within the competence of the BNOC to place orders for new production platforms in certain fields should the Corporation assume a controlling interest in developing fields.

Mr. John Smith: Under Clause 2 of the Petroleum and Submarine Pipe-Lines Bill, the corporation will be empowered to place orders for production platforms. However, the BNOC's use of these powers in relation to any particular project will depend amongst other factors on its position within a licence and the operational arrangements agreed with licensees.

Mr. Gordon Wilson asked the Secretary of State for Energy what is the policy of
725 his Department regarding a possible large-scale increase in road lighting cuts by local authorities during the next fiscal year; whether he is satisfied that the cuts already carried out will not endanger public safety; and if he will make a statement.
Dr. Gilbert: I have been asked to reply.
I will write to the hon. Member.

Mr. Ralph Howell asked the Secretary of State for Energy if the cost of his visit to Tokyo was met by the International Metal Workers' Federation; and what proportion of the expenses of this trip will be paid from public funds.

Mr. Benn: The International Metalworkers invited me to speak at their conference in Tokyo and offered to pay the return fare. Since this visit gave me the opportunity for discussions with the Japanese Foreign Minister, Minister of International Trade and Industry and senior officials the fare was, in accordance with the normal rules concerning Ministers travelling abroad on Government business, met from public funds.

Mr. Hannam asked the Secretary of State for Energy if he will list the numbers and titles of directives issued by circular from the Department of Energy since February 1974 which involved local authorities in additional expenditure.
Mr. Eadie: There is none.

Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of State for Energy how many staff were employed by his Department in February 1974, October 1974, and at the most recent date for which figures are available; and what increases he anticipates for the rest of this year and 1976.
Mr. Benn: The number of staff employed by my Department in February 1974, October 1974 and October 1975 was 1,422, 1,794 and 1,384 respectively.

The figure for February 1974 does not include staff engaged mainly on common services who had not, at that time, been transferred from the Department of Trade and Industry: both the 1974 figures in- 726 clude some 680 staff transferred to the Health and Safety Executive on 1st January 1975 and thus not included in the October 1975 figure.
Any further increase in the staff of my Department by the end of 1976 is expected to be minimal.
Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of Stale for Energy what is the total wage and salary bill of his Department and the proportion resulting from the employment of additional staff since February 1974.

Mr. Benn: The total annual salary bill of the present staff of my Department amounts to approximately £6·7 million of which slightly under half results from the employment of additional staff since February 1974, when some functions were still to be transferred from Department of Trade and Industry. The salaries of staff transferred to the Health and Safety Executive on 1st January 1975 have been left out of the above calculation.

Mr. Hannam asked the Secretary of State for Energy how many public relations and information officers were employed by the Department of Energy and its associated agencies in February 1974; how many are employed now; whether he expects to recruit any more during the rest of 1975 and 1976; and what are the salaries of those he has recruited and expects to recruit.

Mr. Benn: In February 1974 there were eight information officers employed in my Department; certain services were still being provided at that time by the Department of Trade and Industry. This figure has since risen to 23 and I expect a further six to be recruited by April 1977. The total annual salary bill of the present staff amounts to £132,000 and this will be increased by £34,000 when the remaining six posts are filled.
No public relations officers are employed in the Department.

Mr. Viggers asked the Secretary of State for Energy how many miles of pipe are represented by the figures of £6·1 million for 1974 and £1·6 million for the first
727 half of 1975 which were stated to be the value of orders placed with the United Kingdom producers in the Secretary of State's reply to the hon. Member for Gosport's Question to which an answer was given on Wednesday 15th October.

Mr. John Smith: It is not possible to quantify the mileage of pipe involved in these orders since much of it is used in comparatively short lengths in terminal facilities, on production platforms and for conductor pipes, casing and associated drill pipe.

Mr. Viggers asked the Secretary of State for Energy what is the approximate cost of the 1,200 miles of submarine pipeline stated by the Secretary of State to be required to complete the development of existing commercial discoveries in the United Kingdom sector of the North Sea in his answer to the hon. Member for Gosport's Question to which a reply was made on 15th October.
Mr. John Smith: The cost of the pipe itself would be about £300 million at today's prices. The cost of pipe-coating, trenching, laying and covering would add at least a further £600 million.

Mr. Viggers asked the Secretary of State for Energy what is his best estimate of the percentage of submarine pipeline required in the United Kingdom sector of the North Sea which is being provided by British producers.

Mr. John Smith: British producers have supplied some 20 per cent. of the submarine pipeline installed so far in this sector. No orders have yet been placed with British producers for any of the 1,200 miles of submarine pipeline that may be required to complete the development of existing commercial discoveries of oil and gas in the United Kingdom sector of the North Sea. Many of the pipelines involved are still at the planning stage.

Mr. Hall-Davis asked the Secretary of State for Energy what arrangements have been made to ensure that the advice of the Nuclear Safety Advisory Committee will be available at all times and on all relevant matters to the Health and Safety 728 Commission; whether the advice will be confined to the safety of those working in nuclear installations; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Benn: The Health and Safety Commission has full access to the Nuclear Safety Advisory Committee and its work. The committee's advice, which is not confined to the safety of workers in nuclear installations, is available to the commission on all aspects of nuclear safety arising from the Nuclear Installations Act 1965.
Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of State for Energy if he will indicate whether any North Sea oilfields or potential hydrocarbon discoveries lie within three miles of the Scottish coast.
Mr. John Smith: There are no such fields: in the light of present knowledge, the possibilities of a discovery are remote.
Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of State for Energy if he will list the number of North Sea oilfields and potential discoveries of hydrocarbons which lie within three miles of the Shetland Islands.
Mr. John Smith: There are no such fields: in the light of present knowledge, the possibilities of a discovery are remote.
Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of State for Energy if he will give a list of the 15 major oilfields of the North Sea and indicate the distance of each from the United Kingdom coastline.

Mr. John Smith: There are 13 commercial fields on the United Kingdom Shelf and these with their distances from the United Kingdom coast are as follows:

Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of State for Energy what he considers to be a fair oil floor price for the North Sea; and how many Community countries, apart from the International Energy Agency, have accepted the need in principle.

Mr. John Smith: Details of the minimum safeguard price scheme are under negotiations, and it would be premature to reveal the price level being discussed; it of course does not only apply to North Sea oil. Those Members of the European Community who are also Members of the International Energy Agency have accepted the principle of the proposed scheme.

Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of State for Energy on the basis of the Secretary of State's statement that there will be no discrimination against foreign companies applying for licences during the next round, whether it is his intention to enable the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics to apply among other European States.

Mr. John Smith: My right hon. Friend's statement on the 10th November may be taken as including State corporations from other countries. Any application will be considered in accordance with the arrangements of the Round to be announced early next year.
Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of State for Energy if he will appoint a firm of industrial consultants to advise the BNOC on the suitability of its structure and the best way to deploy its resources.

Mr. John Smith: BNOC's internal structure and deployment of resources will be matters for the corporation, unless brought to my right hon. Friend's attention as a result of a statutory review of management and organisation under Clause 3 (4) of the Petroleum and Submarine Pipelines Bill.
Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of State for Energy whether he proposes that fur- 730 ther State funds should be used to enable either the National Coal Board or the CEGB to finance coal stocks.
Mr. Eadie: The National Coal Board and the Electricity Council already have access to the National Loans Fund as a source of finance for stocking of coal. This will continue.

Mr. Gordon Wilson asked the Secretary of State for Energy what proportions of total estimated NCB capital expenditure have been earmarked for Scotland in the next five years; and if he will also express the figures in percentage form.

Mr. Eadie: The board informs me that its planned capital expenditure in Scotland for the current financial year—1975–76—is £12 million. This is 5½ per cent. of the board's allocation for capital expenditure on mining for the year.
The board is not able to provide corresponding figures for future years.
Mrs. Bain asked the Secretary of State for Energy what proportion of Scottish households rely on electricity as their principal means of heating.
Mr. William Ross: I have been asked to reply.

I understand from the Scottish electricity boards that about 20 per cent. of the houses in the South Board's area and about 33 per cent. in the North Board's area use electricity for all purposes including cooking and heating.
I am asking the chairmen of the boards to write to the hon. Member with such further information as they may have about the use of electricity for house heating.
Mr. Skeet asked the Secretary of State for Energy what is the terminal limit of the waters off Northern Ireland.
Dr. Summerskill: I have been asked to reply.
The general limit of these territorial waters, as for the rest of the territorial sea adjacent to the United Kingdom, is three miles.
Mr. Gordon Wilson asked the Secretary of State for Energy what agreement was reached with the Isle of Man in respect of its rights to offshore mineral exploitation in the Irish Sea.
Dr. Summerskill: I have been asked to reply.
The Isle of Man is not part of the United Kingdom but a dependency of the Crown with its own system of law and administration.
The Continental Shelf Act 1964 does not confer extra-territorial powers on any Isle of Man authority in respect of the area of sea immediately adjacent to the territorial waters around the Island.

In 1966 Her Majesty's Government, recognising the Island Government's interest in the exploitation of the resources of the continental shelf in that area, entered into an agreement with the Government of the Isle of Man that provides for the Island to benefit from the exploitation of the petroleum resources of the continental shelf.

The general financial arrangements are set out in the Miscellaneous Financial Provisions Act 1968. They provide for the Government of the Isle of Man to receive a share of the licence fees and royalties paid to the Secretary of State under the Petroleum Production Act 1934—as amended by the Continental Shelf Act 1964—in respect of the entire British continental shelf outside territorial waters.

The agreement does not cover the exploitation of minerals other than petroleum; nor does it apply to the exploitation of resources within the territorial waters around the Isle of Man, which is a matter for the Isle of Man Government.

13. Mr. Alexander Wilson asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what discussions he has had regarding the introduction of an independent element in the procedure for dealing with complaints against the police.
Mr. Harry Ewing: Outline proposals for such a scheme have been discussed 732 with the police associations and the Convention of Scottish Local Authorities. These consultations are continuing.
19. Mr. Small asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if he is satisfied with the rate of house building in the private and public sectors; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Hugh D. Brown: I am encouraged by the revival of public sector house building in Scotland over the past year, with more houses approved, started, under construction and completed. Approvals for the year to the end of August are up from 13,416 in 1973–74 to 19,513 in 1974–75. I give below the corresponding figures for houses started, under construction and completed. There are signs also that the private sector is recovering. But much remains to be done in some areas and I shall encourage measures to meet housing needs where-ever they arise.

Following are the figures:—
September 1973—August 1974 September 1974—August 1975
Starts 19,546 20,143
Under construction 30,576 31,165
Completions 15,863 19,554

20. Mr. Buchanan asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if, in view of the number of properties acquired in advance of requirements in the Springburn area and which are now in a derelict condition, he will treat Springburn as a special area for the purpose of central Government assstance, in order to enable developments which are urgently required to be proceeded with despite the prevailing financial situation.
Mr. Millan: I recognise the special problems of Springburn and the need for urgency in tackling them. I shall consider as sympathetically as possible any proposals which require my sanction.
21. Mr. Gourlay asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what representations he has received requesting the use of EEC regional aid funds to construct the East Fife regional road.
Mr. Millan: Fife Regional Council has inquired about the possibility of assistance from these funds.

22. Mr. Adam Hunter asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will bring forward proposals to introduce legislation to abolish the tied house system which adversely affects certain non-industrial and industrial civil servants; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Hugh D. Brown: The official provision of houses for civil servants who work in remote stations or who are required to reside close to their place of work is non-statutory, and there is no need for legislation to alter the present arrangements. The houses are provided for the convenience of the staff as well as the convenience of the Department; and, although there have been a few representations about proposed increases in the rents, I am unaware of any previous suggestion that it would be beneficial to stop providing such houses under present arrangements, and I see no grounds for doing so.
24. Mr. Teddy Taylor asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will make a statement on the level of expenditure on education.
Mr. McElhone: I cannot at present add to the information given in Cmnd 5879 published last January.

25. Mr. Fairbairn asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what plans he has to cut waste in Government expenditure in Scotland and to penalise extravagance and reward economy in the public service in Scotland.
Mr. William Ross: In that part of the public service for which I am responsible I seek to ensure that the resources employed are no more than the efficient conduct of business requires.

Mr. Fairbairn asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what has been the total cost to the Exchequer and the total increase in the local government staff levels since 1974 as a result of the require- 734 ments of new legislation and departmental circulars initiated by his office.

Mr. William Ross: It is not possible to quantify the increase of expenditure in a particular period which has resulted from new legislation or Departmental circulars. The emphasis of Scottish Office circulars during the past year has been on the need to reduce the growth of expenditure, in real terms, and to keep increases in staff complements to a minimum.
26. Mr. Kilroy-Silk asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if he has made any changes in the allocation of responsibilities to Ministers in his Department.

Mr. William Ross: There have been two changes in the ministerial team at the Scottish Office since the beginning of the year, but the allocation of responsibilities among Ministers has not been altered.
27. Mr. Sillars asked the Secretary of State for Scotland when he next plans to meet the STUC and other Scottish organisations concerned with the Scottish economy.

Mr. William Ross: My right hon. Friend the Minister of State met the STUC last Friday and I met it last on 10th October. As always, I am ready to consider any requests for meetings from organisations concerned with the Scottish economy on their merits.
28. Mr. Rifkind asked the Secretary of State for Scotland whether he will make an official visit to the site to be used for the Scottish Assembly.
31. Mr. Reid asked the Secretary of State for Scotland whether he will make an early official visit to the Scottish Assembly site.
Mr. Harry Ewing: My right hon. Friend is familiar with the site and has no plans to make an official visit.
32. Mr. William Hamilton asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will publish a White Paper indicating the estimated cost of establishing and running an elected Scottish Assembly.

Mr. Harry Ewing: As my hon. Friend the Minister of State, Privy Council Office, informed the House on 22nd October, the estimated costs of the Scottish Assembly will be dealt with in the forthcoming White Paper on devolution.

Mr. William Hamilton asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what representations he has received in the last year from individuals or organisations of the desirability of establishing an elected Scottish Assembly with powers and functions completely separate from the rest of the United Kingdom.
Mr. William Ross: In the last year one letter addressed to me from a member of the public advocated such an Assembly.
29. Mrs. Bain asked the Secretary of State for Scotland how many children will leave school at the next leaving date this year.
Mr. McElhone: About 16,000 pupils are expected to leave school at Christmas.
30. Mr. Grimond asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if staff-watch arrangements have been introduced for the Scottish regions; and with what results.

Mr. Millan: It has been agreed with the Convention of Scottish Local Authorities that a system of monitoring local authority staff numbers in Scotland should be introduced, and the arrangements are now under discussion.

Mr. Crawford asked the Secretary of State for Scotland how many people are now employed by the Tayside Regional Council and by the Perth and Kinross District Council; and how many people were employed by Perth Town Council, Perth County Council, and Kinross County Council, respectively, on 1st May 1975.

Mr. William Ross: Details of the numbers of staff employed by individual local authorities are not available. The hon. Member will realise that, even if the figures were available, they would 736 not be comparable, owing to changes in responsibilities.
Mr. Fairbairn asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what was the expenditure on the Scottish Office car pool in 1973–74 and 1974–75; and what is the anticipated expenditure in 1975–76.

Mr. William Ross: Part of the cost of the Scottish Office car pool is charged against a number of departmental services to which vehicles are allocated; and the rest forms part of the expenditure on vehicles generally, including specialist vehicles. Expenditure relating to the car pool alone could not be extracted without disproportionate labour.
Mr. D. E. Thomas asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what proportion of secondary schools in Scotland has appointed school counsellors; and what is the total number of counsellors.

Mr. William Ross: All secondary schools in Scotland under education authority management have appointed teachers with special responsibility for pupil guidance. About 2,700 such teachers were employed in September 1974.
33. Mr. Monro asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what consultations he has had with the Dumfries and Galloway Regional Council concerning future road improvements on the A75.
Mr. Millan: My Department is frequently in touch with the Regional Council on the A75 generally and on particular schemes.

Mr. William Ross: Separate figures are not available for 1966–67 for the areas now comprised by the Western Isles. Figures for 1974–75 are as follows:

Mr. Fairbairn asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what is the number of vacancies in his Department for which recruits are required but which have not yet been filled.
Mr. William Ross: 236, including 137 vacancies in the Scottish Prisons Service.

Mr. Fairbairn asked the Secretary of State for Scotland how many public relations officers were employed by his Department in March 1974; how many are employed now; whether he expects to recruit any more during the rest of 1975 and 1976; and what are the salaries of those he has recruited and expects to recruit.
Mr. William Ross: The Scottish Information Office provides services in Scotland for other Departments as well as my own. In March 1974 the approved complement of the Information Officer

tr.td: * On basis of all teachers employed.

body.p: Group was 24; it is now 28. There were four vacancies in March 1974; there is now one.

Each of the four new posts is offset by a reduction elsewhere—three by reduction in administrative staff now replaced by Information Group staff and one by the transfer of a post from the Department of Industry (Glasgow) when I assumed responsibility for selective assistance to industry in July of this year. The net increase in public service manpower as a result of the increased complement is, therefore, nil. Estimates for staff needs in 1976–77 are now under consideration.

Mr. Fairbairn asked the Secretary of State for Scotland for what reasons any extra staff were recruited in his Department between March 1974 and the present; and for what reasons are any extra staff likely to be recruited for the rest of this year and 1976.

Mr. William Ross: For the reasons for increases in staff from March 1974 to the present I refer to the answer I gave the hon. Member for Melton (Mr. Latham) on 10th November—[Vol. 899, c. 454.] Further increases in 1975–76 will be kept to a minimum and will be within the limits of supply estimates approved by Parliament and for the broad purposes specified in the explanatory notes to the Estimates. Mr. Reid asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will make a statement on his policy towards football vandalism in Scotland.

Mr. William Ross: I have expressed concern many times about the behaviour of spectators at certain sporting occasions. The courts, the police, social workers, teachers and parents all have a part to play in providing a remedy. If the hon. Member has in mind damage to property, I deplore that, too, whether or not it is associated with football crowds. Police strength in Scotland is now higher than it has ever been, but the greatest contribution to reducing this mischief would be a stronger sense of community responsibility, and that it is my object to encourage.

Mr. Reid asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what is his policy towards the notification of all sterilisation operations on under-16 year olds in Scotland and the appointment of local ethical committees to approve such operations as suggested in the Department of Health and Social Security discussion document of 3rd November.
Mr. William Ross: I propose to consider in consultation with the interests concerned whether any advice should be issued on this question.

Mrs. Bain asked the Secretary of State for Scotland how many manufacturing industry factories have closed in Scotland in the year beginning 1st January 1975; in how many cases such factories were branches of (a) the United Kingdom groups and (b) international groups; and how many jobs have been lost in each case to male and female adults, respectively.

Mr. William Ross: The latest information available is that, in the period 1st January 1975 to 31st October 1975, 63 manufacturing establishments closed in Scotland. Of these 56 were owned by United Kingdom companies and seven by overseas groups.

The total number of jobs lost as a result of these closures was approximately 3,200 for males and 2,600 for females. Of these approximately 2,900 males and 2,450 females were employed by United Kingdom companies and 300 males and 150 females by overseas groups.
A breakdown of the figures between jobs for adults and juveniles is not available.
Mr. Henderson asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what guidance he gives to local authorities on the provision of housing to members of the Prison Service who retire or resign.

Mr. William Ross: Local authorities have had their attention drawn to the difficulties which prison service staff experience in obtaining accommodation on retirement and have been asked to give sympathetic consideration to applications for housing from such staff.
Mr. Henderson asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what guidance he gives to local authorities on the provision of housing for ex-Service men.

Mr. William Ross: The latest guidance to local authorities on the allocation of houses for ex-Service men and women is contained in SDD Circular 107/1975. I have arranged for the hon. Member to be provided with a copy.
Mr. Thompson asked the Secretary of State for Scotland what studies he has instituted into the feasibility of making Scotland self-sufficient in timber; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. William Ross: No such studies are in progress, and no separate statistics are maintained of timber consumption in Scotland. The existing area of woodland in Scotland, once it has reached full production about the end of the century, is expected to provide wood sufficient to meet Scotland's estimated share of the present total United Kingdom consumption as calculated pro rata on a population basis, and to allow in addition a margin for increased consumption.
Mr. Crawford asked the Secretary of State for Scotland how many foster parents are in the Tayside Region; and what is the total cost of their remuneration.
Mr. William Ross: I am asking Tayside Regional Council to send this information to the hon. Member.
Mr. Crawford asked the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will introduce a buy Scottish policy in Scottish regional and district councils.
Mr. William Ross: No.

Mr. Hayhoe asked the Secretary of State for Employment how many staff and in what categories have been recruited to his Department since March 1974; and what has been the net change in the total staff employed.

Mr. Booth: The numbers of staff employed in my Department at 1st April 1974 after deducting the estimated numbers employed on functions subsequently transferred to the Manpower Services Commission, Employment Service Agency, Health and Safety Executive and the Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service are shown below together with the comparable figures for 1st October 1975.

In addition, 4,231 casual staff were employed on 1st October 1975 mainly on unemployment benefit work in local offices. It is estimated that on 1st April 1974 some 1,050 casual staff were employed in my Department. It is regretted that comprehensive records of all staff recruited during this period are not available.
Mr. Hayhoe asked the Secretary of State for Employment how many staff, and in what categories, have been
In addition 1,024 casual staff were employed in MSC and its agencies on 1st October 1975. The comparable figure for 1st April 1974 was 1,020.
It is regretted that comprehensive records of all staff recruited during this period are not available.

Mr. Greville Janner asked the Secretary of State for Employment how many prosecutions have been brought since the inception of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act under Section 3 of the Act against employers for failing to take such steps as were reasonably practicable for the safety of persons other than their employees affected by their undertaking and what were the results of such prosecutions.

Mr. Harold Walker: I am informed by the Chairman of the Health and Safety Commission that up to 31st October 1975 no reports had been received of the conclusion of any prosecutions brought under Section 3 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974.

Mr. Greville Janner asked the Secretary of State for Employment how many prosecutions have been brought since the inception of the Health and Safety at Work Act under Section 4 of the Act; and what were the results of such prosecutions.
recruited to the Manpower Services Commission and its agencies since March 1974; and what has been the net change in the total staff employed.

Mr. Booth: I am advised by the Manpower Services Commission that the numbers of staff employed by the Commission and its agencies on 1st April 1974 and on 1st October 1975 are as shown below. The figures for 1st April 1974 include the estimated number of staff employed in the Department of Employment on functions which were transferred to the Commission and its agencies after 1st April 1974.

Mr. Harold Walker: I am informed by the Chairman of the Health and Safety Commission that up to 31st October 1975 one report had been received of a prosecution under Section 4 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The defendant was convicted and fined £5.

Mr. Greville Janner asked the Secretary of State for Employment how many prosecutions have been brought since the inception of the Health and Safety at Work Act under Section 5 of the Act; and what were the results of such prosecutions.

Mr. Harold Walker: I am informed by the Chairman of the Health and Safety Commission that up to 31st October 1975 no prosecutions had been brought under Section 5 of the Health and Safety at Work Etc. Act 1974.

Mr. Greville Janner asked the Secretary of State for Employment how many prosecutions have been brought since the inception of the Health and Safety at Work Act under Section 6 of the Act against designers, manufacturers, importers and suppliers, respectively, of articles or substances; and what were the results of such prosecutions.
Mr. Harold Walker: I am informed by the Chairman of the Health and Safety Commission that up to 31st October 1975

no reports had been received of the conclusion of any prosecutions under Section 6 of the Health and Safety at Work Etc. Act 1974 against designers, manufacturers, importers and suppliers of articles or substances.

Mr. Greville Janner asked the Secretary of State for Employment how many prosecutions have been brought against employees under Section 7 of the Health and Safety at Work Act; how many of these were on indictment; and what were the results of such prosecutions.

Mr. Harold Walker: I am informed by the Chairman of the Health and Safety Commission that up to 31st October 1975 no reports had been received of the conclusion of any prosecutions brought by the Health and Safety Executive against employees under Section 7 of the Health and Safety at Work Etc. Act 1974. Details of prosecutions taken by local authorities are not available.

Mr. Greville Janner asked the Secretary, of State for Employment how many prosecutions have been brought since the inception of the Health and Safety at Work Act under Section 2 of the Act against employers for failing to take such steps as were reasonably practicable for the safety of employees; how many and what percentage of such prosecutions were on indictment; how many and what percentage of such prosecutions were brought against individuals; in how many and what percentage of such cases were prosecutions also brought against their employing company or authority; and what were the results of such prosecutions.

Mr. Harold Walker: I am informed by the Chairman of the Health and Safety Commission that up to 31st October 1975 the number of prosecutions reported under Section 2 of the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 against employers for failing to take such steps as are reasonably practicable to ensure the safety of their employees was 12. A conviction was obtained in each case and fines imposed ranging from £40 to £400. All the prosecutions were brought against employing companies. None was taken on indictment.

Mr. Frank R. White asked the Secretary of State for Employment how many people, and for how long over the last 12 months period's quarterly figures, have been made redundant, temporarily laid off or on short-time working, in the Bury and Radcliffe area.
Mr. John Fraser: I am informed by the Manpower Services Commission that redundancies involving the following numbers of people were recorded in the Bury travel-to-work area during the last 12 months.
My Department knows of 700 workers who are currently on short time in the Bury travel-to-work area. Comparable figures for earlier dates are not available.

Mr. McNamara asked the Secretary of State for Employment if he will take steps to ensure that the Health and Safety at Work etc., Act is fully enforced in respect of the election of workers' safety representatives on board trawlers.

Mr. Harold Walker: The section of the Health and Safety at Work Act relating to the election of workers' safety representatives, Section 2(5), is due to be repealed when the Employment Protection Bill is enacted. However, Section 2(4) of the Act empowers the Secretary of State to make regulations providing for the appointment in prescribed cases by recognised trade unions of safety representatives from among the employees. It is for the Health and Safety Commission to put forward to the Secretary of State proposals for such regulations, having first consulted widely with interested parties, and I am advised by the Chairman of the Commission that a consultative document covering this subject will shortly be published. No doubt those bodies concerned
755 with the fishing industry will wish to consider very carefully the question of the suitability of the Commission's proposals for application to that industry.

Mr. Leslie Spriggs asked the Secretary of State for Employment what are the latest figures, both in absolute and percentage terms, for unemployed men, women and school leavers in Scotland, England and Wales, indicating separately figures and percentages for Merseyside

Mr. John Fraser: This information is not readily available and could not be obtained without disproportionate cost. On 9th October 1975 there were a total of 6,326 school leavers registered as unemployed in the Merseyside metropolitan county, but the statistics do not
as a whole and for each employment office in the Merseyside Metropolitan County Council area.

Mr. John Fraser: Rates of unemployment are calculated by expressing the numbers unemployed as a percentage of the estimated number of employees, employed and unemployed. Rates can be calculated for complete travel-to-work areas but not for their constituent parts. Separate percentage rates of unemployment are not available for school leavers. Following is the information available.
define the date of leaving school. Comparable figures for previous Octobers are as follows:
Records for the years 1970 and 1971 are not readily available.

Mr. Gwilym Roberts asked the Secretary of State for Employment what study he has made of the evidence of high unemployment in Cannock and Rugeley which has been supplied to him; and if he will take steps to give special help to pockets of very high unemployment outside the development and intermediate area.

Mr. John Fraser: I am aware of the unemployment situation in Cannock and Rugeley and my officials are at present studying a number of reports which have a bearing on this. I am also conscious of the general problems associated with pockets of high unemployment outside the assisted areas. The measures announced on 24th September were designed to mitigate the worst effects of high unemployment wherever these occurred. In particular, the temporary employment subsidy was extended to the country as a whole.
